cau_hoi: What force causes an apple to fall from a tree to the ground?
giai_thich: The Earth pulls everything towards its center. According to legend, Isaac Newton conceived the law of universal gravitation when he saw an apple fall in his garden in Woolsthorpe (England) around 1666. He realized that the same force pulling the apple down also keeps the Moon in orbit around the Earth. The apple tree is still alive, and its branches have been grafted and planted in many places around the world.

cau_hoi: During a thunderstorm, why do we often see lightning before we hear thunder?
A: The eye is faster than the ear
C: Thunder occurs a few minutes after lightning
D: Light travels much faster than sound
giai_thich: Light travels at about 300,000 km per second, reaching our eyes almost instantly, while sound in air travels at only about 340 m per second. A good tip: count the seconds from when you see lightning to when you hear thunder and divide by 3 to know the distance to the lightning in kilometers. In fact, lightning and thunder occur simultaneously; thunder is the sound of air being suddenly heated.

cau_hoi: What happens when two like poles of two magnets (north with north) are brought close together?
B: They have no effect on each other
giai_thich: Like poles repel each other, while unlike poles attract. The Earth is similar to a giant magnet, which is why a compass needle always points north-south. Interestingly, the magnetic pole near the geographic North Pole is actually a magnetic south pole because it attracts the north pole of the compass needle. If you cut a magnet in half, you get two new magnets, each still having both poles.

cau_hoi: At normal pressure at sea level, at what temperature does water boil?
giai_thich: Swedish astronomer Anders Celsius proposed his temperature scale in 1742, using the freezing and boiling points of water as reference points. At high altitudes, the air pressure is lower, so water boils at a lower temperature: at the summit of Everest, it is only about 70°C, making it difficult to boil eggs. A pressure cooker does the opposite: it increases pressure so that water boils at around 120°C, helping to cook faster.

cau_hoi: Why can a ship made of iron weighing thousands of tons still float on water?
B: Because iron is lighter than water
C: Because there is a motor keeping the ship up
D: The hollow body of the ship displaces a large volume of water, so the buoyant force of the water is sufficient to lift the ship
giai_thich: A solid block of iron will sink, but when made into a hollow ship containing a lot of air, it displaces a large amount of water. The water pushes up with a force equal to the weight of the water displaced. When this buoyant force equals the weight of the ship, the ship floats. If water floods into the ship's hull like the Titanic in 1912, the buoyant force is no longer sufficient, and the ship sinks.

cau_hoi: Which of the following materials conducts electricity best and is commonly used as the core of electrical wires?
giai_thich: Copper conducts electricity very well, is easy to draw into wires, and is not too expensive, making it the material used for electrical wires. Silver conducts electricity slightly better than copper but is much more expensive. Plastic and rubber are insulators, used to cover wires to protect users from electric shocks. Therefore, never touch exposed wires, especially with wet hands.

cau_hoi: The unit of force in the International System of Units (SI) is named after which scientist?
giai_thich: One newton (N) is the force needed to accelerate a 1 kg mass by 1 m/s². A small apple weighing about 100 g is pulled by the Earth with a force of about 1 N, which is interestingly consistent with the apple story. Many other units are also named after scientists: joule (energy), watt (power), volt (voltage), ampere (current), kelvin (temperature).

cau_hoi: Why can a plastic comb attract small pieces of paper when combing hair on a dry day?
A: The comb is electrically charged due to friction
giai_thich: When rubbed, electrons transfer from hair to the comb (or vice versa), causing the comb to become electrically charged. Charged objects can attract light materials like scraps of paper. This phenomenon is stronger on dry days because humid air helps dissipate electric charge. This is called static electricity, which is also why we sometimes get a slight 'shock' when touching a metal doorknob or when taking off a wool sweater.

cau_hoi: Why does ice float on water?
D: Ice is lighter (has a lower density) than liquid water because water expands when it freezes
giai_thich: Most substances contract when they solidify, but water expands by about 9% because its molecules arrange into a crystalline structure with many gaps. This allows ice to float on lakes, keeping the water below from freezing completely so that fish can survive the winter. This is also why a water bottle left too long in the freezer can crack.

cau_hoi: What is the phenomenon called when we hear our voice echoing back when shouting loudly in a cave or mountainous area?
giai_thich: Sound reflects when it encounters a hard rock wall and returns to our ears. We can only distinguish the echo from the original sound when the reflected sound arrives at least about 0.1 seconds later, meaning the rock wall must be at least about 17 m away. Bats and dolphins use echolocation to find prey. Ships use sonar to send sound down to the seabed to measure depth.

cau_hoi: Through which medium can sound travel?
C: Air, water, and solids, but cannot travel in a vacuum
giai_thich: Sound is the vibration of particles that requires a medium to travel. In space, which is almost a vacuum, astronauts must communicate via radio waves. Sound travels in water about 4 times faster than in air, and even faster in steel. By placing an ear on the railway, one can hear a train approaching from a distance.

cau_hoi: What type of energy is converted into electrical energy by solar panels?
giai_thich: Solar panels are made from semiconductors like silicon. When sunlight hits them, electrons are freed and generate an electric current. This is a clean and renewable energy source that does not emit greenhouse gases during operation. Vietnam, especially the Central South provinces like the old Ninh Thuan, has abundant sunshine, leading to the development of many solar power plants in recent years.

cau_hoi: A seesaw is an example of which type of simple machine?
giai_thich: A lever consists of a rigid bar that pivots around a fulcrum. A lighter person sitting far from the fulcrum can lift a heavier person sitting close. Tools like crowbars, tongs, fishing rods, and even our arms operate like levers. Archimedes once said, 'Give me a place to stand, and I will move the Earth,' to illustrate the power of the lever.

cau_hoi: When looking at a straw submerged in a glass of water, it appears to be bent at the water's surface. What is this phenomenon called?
giai_thich: Light traveling from water to air changes direction at the boundary because the speed of light in water is about 25% slower than in air. Our eyes perceive light as traveling in a straight line, so the part of the straw underwater appears displaced. Refraction also causes the bottom of a swimming pool to look shallower than it actually is. Fishermen using spears must aim lower than the position of the fish they see.

cau_hoi: When a bus brakes suddenly, passengers lean forward. What causes this?
A: Inertia: the body tends to maintain its motion
D: There is a pulling force from the front
giai_thich: According to Newton's first law, an object in motion will remain in motion unless acted upon by an external force. When the bus stops suddenly, our legs stop with the bus, but our upper body continues moving forward. This is why seatbelts are necessary in cars: at a speed of 50 km/h, a sudden stop is equivalent to falling from a height of about 10 meters.

cau_hoi: How does heat transfer from the hot end to the cold end of a metal spoon placed in a cup of hot tea?
giai_thich: In metals, free electrons move quickly and transfer energy very efficiently, making metals good conductors of heat. Wood, plastic, and air are poor conductors of heat, which is why pot handles are often made of wood or plastic. Convection is how heat transfers in liquids and gases, like boiling water rolling up. Radiation is how heat from the Sun travels through a vacuum to Earth.

cau_hoi: White light passing through a prism separates into many colors. Which scientist conducted the famous experiment proving this in the 1660s?
giai_thich: Newton shone a beam of sunlight through a small hole in a window into a prism and saw a spectrum of colors from red to violet. He also used a second prism to recombine the colors back into white light, proving that the prism does not 'create' colors but merely separates them. He chose to divide them into 7 colors, perhaps to match the 7 musical notes. A rainbow forms in a similar way when light passes through raindrops.

cau_hoi: How does a thermos keep hot water warm for a long time?
D: Two layers of glass or metal with a vacuum layer in between and a silver-coated surface
giai_thich: The vacuum layer prevents heat transfer by conduction and convection, as there are no particles to transfer it. The shiny surface reflects thermal radiation back. The tightly sealed lid prevents steam from escaping. Scottish scientist James Dewar invented the vacuum flask in 1892 to keep extremely cold liquefied gases. Using the same principle, the thermos can also keep cold beverages.

cau_hoi: What is the speed of light in a vacuum approximately?
giai_thich: The exact speed is 299,792,458 m/s. At that speed, light can circle the Earth about 7.5 times in one second. Light from the Moon takes about 1.3 seconds to reach Earth, while light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds. According to Einstein's theory of relativity, no object with mass can reach or exceed this speed.

cau_hoi: What does Albert Einstein's famous formula E = mc² indicate?
A: Mass can be converted into energy and vice versa; a small mass contains enormous energy
giai_thich: E is energy, m is mass, c is the speed of light. Since c² is a very large number, just 1 gram of matter fully converted is equivalent to about 21,000 tons of TNT energy. Einstein published this idea in 1905 when he was only 26 years old and working as a patent office clerk in Switzerland. This formula explains why the Sun and nuclear power plants generate energy.

cau_hoi: Why is the sky blue during the day?
C: Because it reflects the color of the sea
D: The air scatters blue light more than red light
giai_thich: Sunlight contains all colors. The tiny gas molecules in the air scatter shorter wavelengths of light, such as blue, in all directions much more than red light, so we see blue everywhere. This phenomenon is called Rayleigh scattering. At sunset, light passes through a thicker layer of air, most of the blue light has been scattered away, leaving only red and orange to reach our eyes.

cau_hoi: Why do skiers or people walking on snow use wide skis or snowshoes?
B: A larger contact area reduces pressure on the snow, preventing sinking
giai_thich: Pressure is equal to force divided by area. With the same weight, if distributed over a larger area, the pressure is lower. Conversely, a needle's tip or a sharp knife has a very small area, creating high pressure, making it easy to puncture or cut. Camels have wide feet to walk on sand. Tanks and bulldozers use tracks to avoid sinking in mud.

cau_hoi: A simple pendulum with a constant length oscillates, and the time for one complete cycle remains nearly constant even as the amplitude decreases. Who discovered this?
giai_thich: According to legend, in 1583, while still a medical student, Galileo observed a chandelier swinging in the Pisa Cathedral and timed it with his pulse. He realized that the oscillation period does not depend on the amplitude when the angle is small. As a result, in 1656, Christiaan Huygens built the first pendulum clock, which was much more accurate than any previous clocks.

cau_hoi: How does a movable pulley help us lift heavy objects?
A: It helps reduce the pulling force by half, but you have to pull the rope twice as long
giai_thich: With a movable pulley, the object is suspended by two segments of rope, each bearing half the weight. In return, to lift the object by 1 meter, you must pull 2 meters of rope. This is the "golden rule" of mechanics: for every multiple of force gained, there is a corresponding loss in distance, with the work done remaining constant. A system of pulleys allows cranes to lift objects weighing tens of tons.

cau_hoi: Why does a microwave oven heat food?
B: Microwaves cause water molecules in food to vibrate rapidly, generating heat
C: There is fire inside the oven
giai_thich: Microwaves with a frequency of about 2.45 GHz cause water molecules, which have two ends with opposite charges, to continuously oscillate in the electric field. The friction between the molecules generates heat. In 1945, American engineer Percy Spencer discovered that a chocolate bar in his pocket melted while he was working near a radar transmitter, leading to the invention of the microwave oven. Metal objects should not be placed in the oven as they can cause sparks.

cau_hoi: Why should you not seek shelter under a tall, solitary tree during a thunderstorm?
B: Because the tree will fall immediately
C: Lightning often strikes the tallest object, and the current can spread to nearby people
D: Because the tree cools people down
giai_thich: Lightning seeks the shortest path to the ground, so tall, pointed, and solitary objects are more likely to be struck. When lightning strikes a tree, the current can "jump" to nearby people or spread across the ground. The safest place is in a sturdy building or a closed car. The lightning rod invented by Benjamin Franklin safely directs lightning to the ground, protecting buildings.

cau_hoi: Why does a helium balloon rise?
A: Helium is lighter than air, so the buoyant force of the air is greater than the weight of the balloon
C: The wind blows the balloon up
D: Helium pushes the balloon up with electricity
giai_thich: Air also exerts an upward buoyant force on all objects, similar to water, according to Archimedes' principle. Helium is about 7 times lighter than air, so the balloon is lighter than the amount of air it displaces and rises. Hot air balloons use hot air because hot air expands and is lighter than cold air. In 1783, the Montgolfier brothers (France) launched the first manned hot air balloon.

cau_hoi: What does the term "Mach 1" mean?
A: Equal to the speed of a cheetah
B: Equal to the speed of light
C: Equal to the speed of a bicycle
D: Equal to the speed of sound
giai_thich: The Mach number is named after the Austrian physicist Ernst Mach. Near the ground, Mach 1 is about 1,235 km/h, but decreases with altitude because the air is colder. In 1947, American pilot Chuck Yeager flew the Bell X-1 and became the first person to fly faster than sound in a controlled horizontal flight. When an aircraft exceeds the speed of sound, it creates a very loud sonic boom.

cau_hoi: Why are LED bulbs more energy-efficient than traditional incandescent bulbs?
A: Most of the electrical energy is converted into light rather than heat
B: Because LEDs do not require electricity
D: Because LEDs are made of paper
giai_thich: Incandescent bulbs convert only about 5% of electrical energy into light, with the rest turning into heat, making them very hot. LED lights provide the same brightness but use about 1/6 to 1/8 of the electricity and last tens of times longer. In 2014, the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to three Japanese scientists, Akasaki, Amano, and Nakamura, for inventing blue LEDs, which helped create white LED lights.

cau_hoi: Why are convex mirrors often placed at road bends or blind corners in supermarkets?
C: To provide a wider field of view than flat mirrors
giai_thich: Convex mirrors cause light rays to reflect outward, allowing us to see a much wider area than a flat mirror of the same size, even though the image appears smaller. The right-side rearview mirror of cars in many countries has a warning label "objects in mirror are closer than they appear." Conversely, concave mirrors converge light, used in flashlights, telescopes, and solar ovens.

cau_hoi: Which Italian physicist invented the first chemical battery in 1800, with the unit of voltage named after him?
giai_thich: "Volta's column" consists of alternating zinc and copper discs, separated by paper or cloth soaked in saltwater, creating a stable electric current. Previously, Luigi Galvani observed frog legs twitching when touched by two metals and believed it was "animal electricity." Volta proved that electricity actually comes from two different metals. Napoleon was very impressed and made him a count.

cau_hoi: What famous experiment did Benjamin Franklin conduct in 1752 to demonstrate that lightning is an electrical phenomenon?
A: Placing a magnet in the rain
C: Lighting a fire on a mountain
D: Flying a kite with a metal key during a storm
giai_thich: Franklin observed that the strands on the kite string stood up and small sparks flew from the key when he brought his hand close, similar to electricity from a Leyden jar. The experiment was very dangerous: in 1753, scientist Georg Richmann in Russia was struck by lightning while conducting a similar experiment. Franklin also invented the lightning rod and coined the terms "positive charge" and "negative charge."

cau_hoi: In 1820, what did Danish physicist Hans Christian Ørsted discover while giving a lecture?
A: An electric current flowing through a conductor deflects a nearby compass needle
giai_thich: This was the first evidence that electricity and magnetism are related. Just a few months later, André-Marie Ampère in France studied the force between electric current-carrying wires, and the unit of electric current, ampere, was named after him. Ørsted's discovery paved the way for electromagnets, electric motors, and the entire field of electromagnetism. Today, electromagnets are found in doorbells, speakers, and MRI machines.

cau_hoi: What phenomenon did Michael Faraday discover in 1831, which is the principle of modern generators?
D: Electromagnetic induction: a changing magnetic field generates an electric current
giai_thich: Faraday moved a magnet in and out of a coil and observed an electric current appearing. Most of today's electricity, from hydroelectric, thermal, to wind power, is generated by rotating magnets or coils. Faraday came from a poor background, only completed elementary school, and was self-taught while working as a bookbinder. According to a legend, when asked what his invention was good for, he replied that one day the government would tax it.

cau_hoi: The Kelvin temperature scale starts from "absolute zero." What temperature does this correspond to in degrees Celsius?
giai_thich: At absolute zero, particles nearly stop thermal motion, and it cannot be cooled further. The Kelvin scale was proposed by British physicist William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, in 1848. The Kelvin scale does not use "degrees," only written as K. Scientists have cooled atoms to within a billionth of a degree of absolute zero, but have never achieved exactly 0 K.

cau_hoi: How was infrared radiation discovered in 1800 by astronomer William Herschel?
C: Placing a thermometer just outside the red light region of the spectrum from a prism and seeing the temperature rise the most
giai_thich: Herschel wanted to measure the heat of each color of light. He was surprised to find that the area beyond red, where the eye could not see, was the hottest. This is infrared radiation, meaning "below red." Today, infrared is used in TV remote controls, thermal imaging cameras, and temperature guns. A year later, Johann Ritter discovered ultraviolet light beyond the violet region.

cau_hoi: What does Ohm's law state about the relationship between which quantities?
B: Voltage, current, and resistance (U = I × R)
giai_thich: German physicist Georg Simon Ohm published the law in 1827. With the same voltage, a wire with higher resistance will have a smaller current. The resistance of a wire depends on the material, length, and cross-section: the longer and thinner the wire, the greater the resistance. Initially, Ohm's work was dismissed by the German scientific community until the Royal Society of London awarded him a medal in 1841.

cau_hoi: What phenomenon did Austrian physicist Christian Doppler explain in 1842, which we hear when an ambulance passes by?
A: The sound is higher when the source approaches and lower when it moves away
giai_thich: As the sound source approaches, the sound waves are "compressed," increasing the frequency; as it moves away, the waves are "stretched," decreasing the frequency. In 1845, Dutch scientist Buys Ballot tested this by having musicians play horns on a moving train. The Doppler effect is used in police speed guns, weather radar, ultrasound imaging, and helps astronomers detect the expanding universe.

cau_hoi: What device does Pascal's law describe, which helps lift cars in repair shops?
giai_thich: Blaise Pascal (17th century) discovered that pressure applied to a liquid in a closed container is transmitted undiminished in all directions. In a hydraulic jack, applying a small force on a small piston generates a much larger force on a larger piston. Car brakes, excavators, and dental chairs also use this principle. Pascal also invented one of the first mechanical calculators when he was just 19 years old, and the unit of pressure is named after him.

cau_hoi: Why do airplane wings create lift?
A: Because the engine pushes straight up into the sky
B: Because there is helium in the wings
C: The shape and angle of the wings cause the air above to move faster and be pushed down, creating a pressure difference that lifts the airplane
D: Because the airplane is lighter than air
giai_thich: According to Bernoulli's principle, fast-moving air has lower pressure. The curved top of the wing causes the air to move faster, resulting in lower pressure above the wing. At the same time, the angle of the wing forces the airflow down, and according to Newton's third law, the air pushes the wing up. A Boeing 747 needs to reach a speed of about 290 km/h on the runway to take off.

cau_hoi: Why is a car safe for the people inside when struck by lightning?
A: Because the car moves faster than lightning
C: Because rubber tires are completely insulating
D: The metal shell conducts electricity running outside to the ground, like a 'Faraday cage'
giai_thich: Many people think rubber tires protect the car, but lightning can travel several kilometers through the air, so a few centimeters of rubber is insignificant. In fact, the current runs along the metal shell outside and then to the ground. Michael Faraday proved in 1836 that electric charge only distributes on the outer surface of a conductor when he sat inside a strongly charged metal cage without being affected.

cau_hoi: Why do we feel cold when walking out of a pool even though it's hot outside?
C: The water evaporating on the skin takes away heat from the body
D: The air is always colder than water
giai_thich: To evaporate, water needs energy, and it takes energy from our skin. This is how sweat helps cool the body. With wind, water evaporates faster, making it feel colder. Historically, people placed clay jars containing water in breezy areas: the water seeps through the jar's walls and evaporates, keeping the water inside cool. Refrigerators also rely on the evaporation of refrigerants.

cau_hoi: Which formula represents Newton's Second Law?
B: F = m × a (force equals mass times acceleration)
giai_thich: The law states that the greater the force, the faster an object accelerates, and the heavier the object, the harder it is to accelerate. To push a truck as fast as a bicycle, we need a much greater force. Newton presented three laws of motion in his book 'Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy' published in 1687, one of the most important scientific books of all time.

cau_hoi: Newton's Third Law explains why rockets can fly in space, where there is no air to 'push' against. What does that law state?
A: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction
C: All objects fall at the same rate
giai_thich: Rockets expel hot gas backwards at very high speeds, and the gas pushes the rocket forward. No air is needed to push against. In 1920, the New York Times mocked rocket scientist Robert Goddard for claiming rockets could not fly in a vacuum. In 1969, when Apollo 11 set off for the Moon, the paper published a correction.

cau_hoi: According to legend, what did Galileo drop two balls of different weights from the Leaning Tower of Pisa to demonstrate?
B: Heavier objects fall twice as fast
C: Ignoring air resistance, all objects fall at the same rate
giai_thich: Aristotle believed heavier objects fell faster, and people accepted this for nearly 2,000 years. Many historians doubt Galileo actually conducted the experiment at the Tower of Pisa, but he studied falling by rolling balls down an inclined plane. In 1971, astronaut David Scott on Apollo 15 dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon, where there is no air, and both hit the ground at the same time.

cau_hoi: Hooke's Law (1660) describes which property of springs?
A: The extension of a spring is proportional to the force applied, within the elastic limit
B: A spring heats up when stretched
C: A spring always breaks when stretched
D: A spring becomes heavier when stretched
giai_thich: Robert Hooke initially published the law in the form of a Latin riddle 'ceiiinosssttuv' in 1676, and two years later decoded it as 'Ut tensio, sic vis' meaning 'the more it stretches, the more force it exerts'. This was how scientists of that time maintained priority for their inventions without revealing the content. A force gauge measures force based on this law.

cau_hoi: Archimedes' principle states that an object submerged in a fluid experiences an upward buoyant force equal to what?
B: The volume of the fluid in the container
D: The weight of the fluid displaced by the object
giai_thich: If the buoyant force is greater than the weight of the object, the object floats; if less, it sinks. Submarines control their buoyancy by pumping water in or out of ballast tanks. Fish have swim bladders filled with gas to adjust buoyancy. In the Dead Sea, the water is very salty and dense, so the buoyant force is large, allowing people to float on the surface and read a newspaper.

cau_hoi: Why can a person standing on a board resting on many nails not puncture their skin?
A: Because human skin is as hard as steel
B: The weight is distributed over hundreds of nails, so the pressure at each nail is very small
C: Because the person is as light as a feather
D: Because the nails are made of plastic
giai_thich: A single nail can puncture skin because all the force is concentrated on a very small area. But when the weight is distributed over many nails, the pressure at each nail drops below the level that would tear the skin. This is the famous 'bed of nails' demonstration, which relies entirely on physics. Stepping on and off is the most dangerous time, as only a few nails bear the weight.

cau_hoi: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed from one form to another. What law is this?
giai_thich: For example, in a hydroelectric plant, the potential energy of water at a height converts to kinetic energy as the water flows down, then to electrical energy through turbines and generators. A portion always converts to unusable heat. This law was developed by many people in the mid-19th century, including German physician Julius Robert Mayer, who realized this while working as a doctor on a ship to Indonesia. Because of this law, 'perpetual motion machines' cannot exist.

cau_hoi: British physicist James Prescott Joule is famous for which experiment in the 1840s?
B: Dropping a heavy weight to spin a paddle in water and measuring the temperature increase, proving mechanical work converts to heat
giai_thich: Joule came from a brewing family and was very skilled at accurately measuring temperature. He discovered the amount of mechanical work needed to raise the temperature of water by one degree, proving that heat is a form of energy rather than an invisible 'caloric' as many believed. The unit of energy, joule, is named after him. According to legend, during his honeymoon, he even brought a thermometer to measure the water at the foot of a waterfall.

cau_hoi: Which scientist proposed a temperature scale where the boiling point of water is initially 0 degrees and the freezing point is 100 degrees?
giai_thich: Celsius published the scale in 1742 with the milestones reversed from today. Just a few years after his death in 1744, the scale was reversed to its current form, possibly proposed by botanist Carl Linnaeus or others. The Fahrenheit scale (1724), still used in the US, sets the freezing point of water at 32°F and the boiling point at 212°F. The average human body temperature is about 37°C, equivalent to about 98.6°F.

cau_hoi: Why do road builders leave small gaps between sections of bridges or railway tracks?
A: To allow rainwater to flow down
C: To give materials room to expand when hot without warping or cracking
D: To allow trains to run smoother
giai_thich: Most materials expand when heated and contract when cold. A steel bridge 1 km long can lengthen by about 0.5 m when the temperature rises by 40°C. The Eiffel Tower is about 15 cm taller in summer than in winter. The "expansion joints" on bridges help the structure change size safely. Modern tracks are often welded and tensioned beforehand to withstand heat.

cau_hoi: In 1798, what did Henry Cavendish use a sophisticated torsion balance for?
A: To measure the temperature of the Sun
B: To measure the speed of sound
C: To measure the gravitational force between lead spheres and thereby calculate the density of the Earth
giai_thich: The gravitational force between two objects in the laboratory is extremely small, so Cavendish had to place the apparatus in a sealed room and observe it with a telescope from outside to avoid air currents and body temperature causing deviations. His results showed that the Earth is about 5.5 times heavier than water, very close to the current value. Therefore, the experiment is often referred to as the "weighing of the Earth."

cau_hoi: In 1851, Léon Foucault hung a giant pendulum 67 m long in the Panthéon (Paris) to demonstrate what?
D: The Earth rotates on its axis
giai_thich: The plane of oscillation of the pendulum appears to gradually rotate over time, but in fact, the pendulum maintains its plane of oscillation while the Earth rotates beneath it. In Paris, the plane completes a full rotation in about 32 hours; at the poles, it takes about 24 hours, while at the equator, it does not rotate. This is the first visual evidence that everyone can see of the Earth's rotation.

cau_hoi: Why do rice cookers and electric kettles typically have short and thick power cords, and why should multiple high-power devices not be plugged into the same outlet?
A: High-power devices consume strong currents, causing wires and outlets to heat up, which can lead to fires
B: Because long wires make electricity flow slower
giai_thich: According to Joule's law, the heat generated in a conductor is proportional to the square of the current. An electric kettle with a power of about 2,000 W uses nearly 9 A at 220 V. If multiple such devices are plugged into a small extension cord at the same time, the wire can overheat, melt the plastic sheath, and cause a short circuit. Circuit breakers help cut off power when overloaded.

cau_hoi: Which part of a bicycle converts the pedaling motion into the rotational motion of the rear wheel?
giai_thich: The front sprocket is usually larger than the rear cassette, so each pedal stroke causes the rear wheel to rotate more times, helping to go faster. When climbing hills, a cyclist shifts to a larger cassette to pedal easier but slower, following the "golden rule" of mechanics. Bicycles are one of the most efficient modes of transport: cyclists expend less energy per km than walking.

cau_hoi: Why does a small boat move backward when a heavy object is thrown forward from it?
B: Because the boat is too light and moves back by itself
C: Due to the conservation of momentum: the object moves in one direction while the boat moves in the opposite direction
giai_thich: Momentum is mass times velocity. Before throwing, the total momentum is zero. After throwing, the momentum of the object moving forward must be balanced by the momentum of the person and the boat moving backward. By the same principle, a gun recoils when fired, a fire hose needs several people to hold it, and squids move by expelling water backward.

cau_hoi: What does a figure skater do to spin faster while rotating?
D: Pull their arms close to their body
giai_thich: This is the law of conservation of angular momentum. When the mass of the body is concentrated closer to the axis of rotation, the spinning speed must increase to compensate. Skilled skaters can spin up to about 6 times per second. To stop, they spread their arms out. Cats also rotate in mid-air by extending and retracting their legs. Stars collapsing into neutron stars can spin hundreds of times per second.

cau_hoi: What force keeps a car on a curved path without skidding out when it goes around a corner?
A: The gravitational force of the Earth
B: The frictional force between the tires and the road, acting as the centripetal force
C: The gravitational force of the Moon
D: The pushing force of the wind
giai_thich: To follow a circular path, an object needs a force directed towards the center of the curve. When the road is slippery due to rain, oil, or ice, friction decreases, and the car is more likely to skid out. Therefore, racetracks and highways at curves are often banked inward to assist. When we spin a bucket of water over our head quickly, the water doesn't spill out thanks to the centripetal force exerted by the bottom of the bucket.

cau_hoi: Why does the sun appear larger and redder when it rises and sets compared to when it is overhead?
A: The red color is due to light passing through a thick layer of atmosphere, scattering away blue light; the feeling of it being larger is mainly an illusion of the brain
B: Because at that time the Sun is closer to the Earth
C: Because the Sun heats up in the morning
giai_thich: If measured with a camera, the size of the Sun or Moon at the horizon is almost the same as when it is high in the sky. Our brain compares them to distant trees and buildings, making us "think" they are larger. This phenomenon is called the Moon illusion, and scientists still debate the exact explanation. The red color has a clear explanation of Rayleigh scattering.

cau_hoi: In 1665 – 1666, when Cambridge University closed due to the plague, what great ideas did Isaac Newton have while he returned to his hometown?
C: Calculus, the theory of color light, and the idea of gravity
giai_thich: This period is often referred to as Newton's "year of wonders," when he was about 23 – 24 years old. Many ideas were only published by him decades later. Regarding calculus, Newton had a fierce dispute with the German mathematician Leibniz, who independently developed it; today we use Leibniz's notation. Newton also built the first reflecting telescope using mirrors.

cau_hoi: What idea about the nature of light did Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens propose in 1678, contrary to Newton's view?
C: Light is made of tiny particles
giai_thich: Newton believed that light consisted of "particles," while Huygens argued that light propagates like waves. Due to Newton's great prestige, the particle theory dominated for over 100 years. In 1801, Thomas Young's double-slit experiment showed that light interferes like water waves. In the early 20th century, Einstein pointed out that light also has particle properties (photons). Today we know that light has both characteristics.

cau_hoi: Where does a rainbow typically appear in the sky in relation to the Sun?
B: On the opposite side of the Sun, when the Sun is behind the observer
giai_thich: Light enters a raindrop, refracts, reflects off the back of the droplet, and then exits, bending about 42° from the opposite direction of the sunlight. Therefore, a rainbow is a circle centered on the shadow of the observer. When the Sun is higher than 42°, a rainbow cannot be seen on the ground, so rainbows typically appear in the early morning or late afternoon. From an airplane, a complete circular rainbow can sometimes be seen.

cau_hoi: When rubbing a balloon on hair and bringing it close to a thin stream of water from a faucet, why does the water bend towards the balloon?
A: Due to wind from the balloon
B: The water is afraid of the balloon
D: The balloon is electrically charged, attracting water molecules, which have two ends with opposite charges
giai_thich: Water molecules have a slightly negative oxygen end and a slightly positive hydrogen end. When an electrically charged object is brought close, the molecules rotate their opposite ends towards the object and are attracted. This simple experiment shows that water is a polar molecule, a property that explains why water can dissolve salt, sugar, and many other substances. The experiment works better on dry days than on humid ones.

cau_hoi: Why do climbers on Everest need to carry oxygen tanks?
A: Because the air on the mountain is all helium
B: At high altitudes, air pressure decreases, and each breath contains much fewer oxygen molecules
C: Because oxygen on the mountain is frozen
D: Because the air on the mountain is toxic
giai_thich: The oxygen ratio in the air remains about 21% at all altitudes, but at the summit of Everest, the pressure is only about one-third of that at sea level, so the amount of oxygen inhaled with each breath is also only about one-third. In 1978, Reinhold Messner and Peter Habeler were the first to reach the summit of Everest without using oxygen tanks. Passenger planes must pressurize the cabin because they fly at altitudes of about 10 – 12 km.

cau_hoi: On a cold morning, why does touching a metal railing feel colder than touching a wooden chair, even though both are at the same temperature?
A: Metal conducts heat well, so it draws heat from our hands faster than wood
B: Our hands feel warmer when touching wood
D: Metal is always colder than wood
giai_thich: Our skin does not directly sense the temperature of an object, but rather the rate of heat transfer away from the skin. Metal conducts heat hundreds of times better than wood, so it quickly draws heat from the hand, creating a chilling sensation. Conversely, on a hot day, a metal chair can burn the hand while a wooden chair feels only warm. Therefore, a tiled floor feels cooler than a wooden or carpeted floor.

cau_hoi: Why do birds sitting on a high-voltage wire not get electrocuted?
A: Because the birds are too light
B: Because the wire has no electricity
D: Both of the bird's feet are on the same wire, so there is almost no voltage difference between the two feet, and current does not flow through the bird's body
giai_thich: Electric current only flows through an object when there is a voltage difference between two points of that object. If a large bird touches two different wires at the same time, or touches a wire and a grounded pole, it will get electrocuted. This is why many utility poles are designed with a wide enough distance between wires to protect large birds like eagles and storks. Humans should never touch power lines, as standing on the ground is already grounded.

cau_hoi: What frequency range can the human ear hear?
giai_thich: Sounds with frequencies below 20 Hz are called infrasound, while those above 20,000 Hz are called ultrasound. Elephants communicate using infrasound that travels several kilometers, while bats and dolphins use ultrasound. As people age, their ability to hear high-frequency sounds decreases, so some high-frequency sounds that students can hear clearly may not be audible to adults. Ultrasound machines in hospitals use frequencies in the millions of Hz to create images inside the body.

cau_hoi: What harm can sounds around 120 decibels (dB), such as the noise of a nearby jet engine, cause?
C: Can cause ear pain and rapid hearing damage
giai_thich: The decibel scale is logarithmic: every increase of 10 dB increases the sound intensity by 10 times. Normal conversation is about 60 dB, while heavy traffic is around 80 – 85 dB. Listening to sounds above 85 dB for many hours can cause long-term ear damage. When using headphones, it is advisable to keep the volume below about 60% of the maximum level and take regular breaks, as hearing damage is often irreversible.

cau_hoi: What type of wave do mobile phones use to transmit call signals to the base station?
B: Radio waves (a type of electromagnetic wave)
giai_thich: Radio waves are in the same family as light, X-rays, and microwaves, differing only in wavelength, and all travel at the speed of light. Mobile phones convert voice into digital signals and then encode them into radio waves. The 5G network uses higher frequencies than older networks, allowing for more data transmission but covering shorter distances, requiring more base stations. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth also use radio waves.

cau_hoi: Why do car tires need grooves, and why are worn smooth tires very dangerous in the rain?
B: Grooves help make the tire lighter
C: Grooves make the car go faster
D: Grooves help drain water and increase friction with the road; smooth tires can easily hydroplane
giai_thich: When the road is wet, a thin layer of water can sit between the tire and the road, causing the car to 'glide' on the water like a skateboard, known as hydroplaning. The grooves channel water away to the sides so the tire can still grip the road. In contrast, Formula 1 cars use slick tires when it's dry for maximum contact area, only switching to grooved tires when it rains.

cau_hoi: In 1865, James Clerk Maxwell published a set of equations describing electricity and magnetism, predicting what about light?
giai_thich: Maxwell calculated the speed of electromagnetic waves in a vacuum and found it matched the measured speed of light. He concluded that light is indeed electromagnetic waves. This is one of the greatest unifications in physics. Einstein hung a picture of Maxwell alongside Newton and Faraday in his office. Maxwell also took the first color photograph in 1861, a photo of a tartan ribbon.

cau_hoi: In 1887, which German physicist first created and detected radio waves in the laboratory, with the frequency unit named after him?
giai_thich: Hertz used an electric spark between two metal spheres to create waves, and a loop with a small gap on the other side of the room produced small sparks, proving that waves had transmitted through space, just as Maxwell predicted. When asked what this discovery was useful for, Hertz is said to have replied, 'not at all.' Just about 14 years later, radio waves crossed the Atlantic.

cau_hoi: In 1901, Guglielmo Marconi successfully transmitted a radio signal across the Atlantic. What was the first signal?
C: The letter 'S' in Morse code (three short beeps)
giai_thich: The signal was transmitted from Poldhu (Cornwall, England) and received by Marconi in St. John's (Newfoundland) using an antenna suspended from a kite. Many scientists thought radio waves traveled in a straight line and could not overcome the curvature of the Earth. Later, it was discovered that the ionosphere reflected radio waves. Marconi won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1909. In 1912, radio helped save over 700 survivors from the Titanic.

cau_hoi: "The War of Currents" at the end of the 19th century in America was a competition between which two types of current?
B: Direct current (Edison) and alternating current (Tesla, Westinghouse)
giai_thich: Edison supported direct current, but it was difficult to transmit over long distances. Nikola Tesla and George Westinghouse developed alternating current, which could use transformers to raise the voltage very high for long-distance transmission with minimal loss. In 1893, alternating current won the bid to light the Chicago World's Fair, and in 1895, the Niagara Falls hydroelectric plant used Tesla's system. Today, most of the world's power grids use alternating current.

cau_hoi: In 1896, Henri Becquerel discovered radioactivity by what coincidence?
A: Uranium salt left in a drawer with a black paper-wrapped photographic plate fogged the plate even without light
B: Hearing a noise from uranium ore
D: Getting burned while holding the ore
giai_thich: Becquerel thought uranium salt needed sunlight to emit rays, but Paris was cloudy, so he stored it in a drawer. When he developed the photographic plate, he was surprised to see a clear image. Uranium emits rays without needing energy from outside. Two years later, Marie and Pierre Curie named the phenomenon 'radioactivity' and discovered polonium and radium. All three shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903.

cau_hoi: In 1897, J. J. Thomson discovered which particle, the first known particle smaller than an atom?
giai_thich: Thomson studied cathode rays in a glass tube from which most of the air had been removed and demonstrated that they consisted of negatively charged particles lighter than hydrogen atoms by about 1,800 times. He proposed the 'plum pudding' model of the atom, with electrons scattered throughout a positively charged mass. Thomson mentored many scientists, including 8 who later won Nobel Prizes, and his own son also won the Nobel Prize in Physics.

cau_hoi: What discovery did the 'gold foil' experiment directed by Ernest Rutherford (1909 – 1911) lead to?
A: Atoms have a very small, dense, positively charged nucleus at the center
giai_thich: Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden fired alpha particles at a thin sheet of gold. Most passed through, but a very few bounced back. Rutherford said this was as astonishing as firing a cannonball at a thin sheet of paper and having it bounce back at you. He concluded that nearly all the mass of an atom is concentrated in a very small nucleus. If an atom were the size of a stadium, the nucleus would be like a pea in the middle of the field.

cau_hoi: In 1913, how did Niels Bohr propose electrons move in his atomic model?
C: On defined energy levels, emitting or absorbing light when jumping between levels
giai_thich: Bohr's model explained why hot hydrogen gas only emits certain colors of light, like the lines in a spectrum. Each element has its own 'spectral fingerprint,' helping astronomers know what substances stars are made of. Bohr won the Nobel Prize in 1922. During World War II, he escaped from occupied Denmark; legend has it he dissolved the Nobel medals of two colleagues in acid to hide them.

cau_hoi: In 1900, what revolutionary idea did Max Planck propose, marking the beginning of quantum physics?
D: Energy is emitted and absorbed in discrete 'packets' called quanta
giai_thich: Planck was trying to explain the light emitted from hot objects (black body radiation). He pointed out the correct formula when assuming energy could only take on values that are multiples of a small quantity, proportional to frequency. Planck's constant is extremely small, about 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s. Planck initially considered it just a 'mathematical trick.' When he was young, a professor advised him not to study physics because 'everything had already been discovered.'

cau_hoi: Albert Einstein won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921 for which work?
giai_thich: When light is shone on certain metals, electrons are emitted. Strangely, red light, no matter how strong, does not cause electrons to be emitted, while weak violet light does. Einstein explained in 1905 that light consists of energy packets (photons), and the energy of each packet depends on the color. The theory of relativity was still controversial at that time, so it was not mentioned as the reason for the award. The photoelectric effect is the principle behind solar panels and camera sensors.

cau_hoi: 1905 is called Einstein's "miraculous year" because he published how many important papers that changed physics?
D: Four papers: photoelectric effect, Brownian motion, special relativity, and E = mc²
giai_thich: At that time, Einstein was 26 years old, a third-class technical expert at the Bern Patent Office (Switzerland), not working at any university. The paper on Brownian motion, the chaotic movement of pollen particles in water, provided compelling evidence for the existence of atoms. In 2005, exactly 100 years later, it was chosen by the United Nations as the International Year of Physics.

cau_hoi: What did Thomas Young's double-slit experiment in 1801 demonstrate about light?
A: Light has wave properties because it creates alternating bright and dark interference patterns
C: Light does not travel in a straight line
giai_thich: When light passes through two narrow slits, alternating bright and dark stripes appear on the screen, similar to two groups of water waves meeting, where wave peaks meet peaks to strengthen, and peaks meet troughs to cancel out. Young was a multi-talented genius: he spoke many languages, was a doctor, and contributed to deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs. In the 20th century, the double-slit experiment with individual electrons became the "central mystery" of quantum mechanics.

cau_hoi: In 1676, Danish astronomer Ole Rømer first demonstrated that light has a finite speed by observing what?
C: The timing of Jupiter's moon Io being eclipsed earlier or later depending on Earth's distance from Jupiter
D: The shadow of a church tower
giai_thich: When Earth is far from Jupiter, light has to travel a longer distance, so Io appears to be delayed by about 22 minutes (actually about 16-17 minutes). Before Rømer, many, including Descartes, believed that light traveled instantaneously. His first estimate based on his data gave a speed of about 220,000 km/s, with the main error due to the distances between planets not being accurately measured at that time.

cau_hoi: In 1887, the Michelson-Morley experiment searched for "ether," the medium believed to transmit light. What was the result?
A: No difference in the speed of light was detected in different directions
C: Light was twice as fast in the north direction
giai_thich: Scientists believed that light was a wave and therefore needed a medium to travel, just as sound needs air. As Earth moved through the ether, light traveling in different directions would have different speeds. Michelson and Morley used an extremely sensitive interferometer placed on a floating block in mercury, but saw no difference. This famous "failure" in history was later explained by Einstein's theory of relativity.

cau_hoi: French military engineer Sadi Carnot laid the foundation for which field in his 1824 book?
D: Thermodynamics, with the theory of maximum efficiency of heat engines
giai_thich: Carnot wanted to know why British steam engines were better than French ones and whether there was a limit to efficiency. He pointed out that maximum efficiency depends only on the temperature difference between the hot and cold sources. No engine can convert all heat into work. Carnot died in 1832 at the age of 36 from cholera, and most of his papers were burned due to quarantine regulations.

cau_hoi: German physicist Rudolf Clausius coined the term "entropy" in 1865. What does the second law of thermodynamics say about entropy?
A: Entropy decreases when it is cold
B: In an isolated system, entropy (degree of disorder) never decreases over time
giai_thich: This is why heat always transfers from hot objects to cold ones, a glass of ice water melts in a room without ever freezing back, and a room tends to become messy rather than tidy. We can reduce entropy in one place, such as a refrigerator cooling food, but it requires energy and increases entropy elsewhere more than it decreases it. Many scientists believe this law explains the "arrow of time."

cau_hoi: Boyle's law (1662) describes what relationship between pressure and volume of a gas at constant temperature?
C: Pressure increases as volume decreases inversely
D: Pressure and volume are always equal
giai_thich: When pushing the piston of a sealed syringe, we find that the harder we push, the more the gas pushes back. If the volume is halved, the pressure doubles. Robert Boyle was an Irish chemist, considered one of the founders of modern chemistry. The law explains why divers must exhale when surfacing quickly: the air in their lungs expands as water pressure decreases.

cau_hoi: In 1643, Evangelista Torricelli, a student of Galileo, invented which instrument?
giai_thich: Torricelli inverted a glass tube about 1 meter long filled with mercury into a basin of mercury. The mercury column fell to about 76 cm, leaving a space above, which was the first artificial vacuum. Atmospheric pressure supports that mercury column. He noticed that the height of the column changed with the weather. His famous quote: "We live at the bottom of an ocean of air."

cau_hoi: In 1654, Otto von Guericke conducted the famous "Magdeburg hemispheres" experiment. What was it?
A: Dropping a ball into a river
B: Dropping a ball from a tall tower
D: Removing all air between two metal hemispheres, and two teams of horses could not pull them apart
giai_thich: When the inside is a vacuum, the outside air pressure presses the two hemispheres tightly together with great force. According to records, two teams of eight horses each could not pull them apart. When the valve was opened to let air in, the two halves easily separated. The experiment was demonstrated before Holy Roman Emperor Ferdinand III. Guericke was also the mayor of Magdeburg and invented the vacuum pump.

cau_hoi: In 1600, the English doctor William Gilbert published the book "De Magnete" with what important conclusion?
B: The Earth is a giant magnet, so the compass needle points north
D: The Earth is the center of the universe
giai_thich: Previously, it was believed that the compass was attracted by the North Star or magnetic mountains in the North. Gilbert made a small magnetic globe called "terrella" (little Earth) and showed that a compass placed on it worked just like on Earth. He also coined the term "electricus" (from the Greek meaning amber), the origin of the word "electricity" today.

cau_hoi: The French scientist Charles-Augustin de Coulomb used a torsion balance in 1785 to discover what law?
C: The force of attraction or repulsion between two charges is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them
giai_thich: Coulomb's law has a form very similar to Newton's law of universal gravitation, but the electric force is much stronger than gravitational force: between two electrons, the electric repulsion is about 10⁴² times stronger than the gravitational attraction. Therefore, a small magnet can lift a pin even though the entire Earth is pulling it down. The unit of electric charge, coulomb (C), is named after him.

cau_hoi: "Leyden jar", invented in 1745 – 1746 in the Netherlands and Germany, is what kind of device?
B: The first device to store electricity, a precursor to the capacitor
giai_thich: The glass jar is coated with metal foil both inside and outside, capable of storing a large amount of electricity and releasing a strong shock. In France, the abbot Nollet once had about 180 soldiers, then hundreds of monks hold hands in a circle and let the current from the Leyden jar pass through; they all jumped at once. Today, capacitors are found in most electronic devices like phones and computers.

cau_hoi: What phenomenon causes a small droplet of water on a very hot pan (over about 200°C) to roll around and persist for a long time instead of evaporating immediately?
A: Leidenfrost effect: the layer of steam underneath makes the droplet "float" and insulates it from the pan
giai_thich: The German scientist Johann Gottlob Leidenfrost described this phenomenon in 1756. When the pan is extremely hot, the bottom of the droplet evaporates immediately, creating a thin vapor cushion that allows the droplet to glide like a hovercraft. At lower temperatures, around 100 – 150°C, the droplet makes direct contact with the pan and evaporates faster. Chefs use this trick to know if the pan is hot enough.

cau_hoi: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge (USA) collapsed in 1940 just a few months after its opening due to what physical phenomenon?
C: Wind-induced oscillation (elastic wave shaking) causing the bridge deck to twist violently until it broke
giai_thich: The bridge was nicknamed "Galloping Gertie" because the deck often undulated up and down in the wind. On November 7, 1940, winds of about 64 km/h caused the deck to twist violently and then collapse into the river, and the scene was filmed. There were no fatalities, only a dog. This event completely changed the way suspension bridges were designed, and engineers began testing bridge models in wind tunnels.

cau_hoi: When the Millennium Bridge for pedestrians in London was inaugurated in 2000, it shook violently and had to be closed. What was the cause?
D: Small lateral oscillations causing pedestrians to unconsciously step in sync, amplifying the oscillation
giai_thich: When the bridge swayed slightly sideways, pedestrians automatically spread their legs and stepped in rhythm with the sway to maintain balance. Thousands of people stepping in sync caused the bridge to sway even more, creating a feedback loop. The bridge was closed after two days and about 90 dampers were installed, reopening in 2002. Londoners nicknamed it "The Wobbly Bridge."

cau_hoi: In 2009, Chinese-born scientist Charles Kao received the Nobel Prize in Physics for what contribution?
B: Researching light transmission in optical fibers, the foundation of high-speed Internet
giai_thich: In 1966, Kao calculated that if impurities in glass could be removed, light could travel very far in optical fibers. Light travels in optical fibers due to total internal reflection, continuously bouncing off the walls of the fiber without escaping. Today, millions of kilometers of underwater fiber optic cables connect continents, carrying most Internet data. Kao is referred to as the "father of fiber optics."

cau_hoi: Why does a diamond sparkle much more than a piece of glass cut in the same shape?
A: Diamonds have a very high refractive index, causing multiple total internal reflections and splitting light into many colors
giai_thich: The refractive index of diamond is about 2.42, much higher than that of ordinary glass (about 1.5), so the critical angle is only about 24°. Light entering a properly cut diamond reflects multiple times inside and then escapes upwards. Diamonds also exhibit strong dispersion, creating small rainbow-colored rays called "fire." The round cut with 57 – 58 facets is designed to optimize this phenomenon.

cau_hoi: How did the French physicist Hippolyte Fizeau measure the speed of light on the ground in 1849?
B: Measuring the shadow of the Moon
D: Shining light through a gap in a rapidly rotating gear to a mirror about 8 km away and measuring the rotation speed to block the light with the teeth
giai_thich: When the gear rotates fast enough, light passes through a gap, reflects off the mirror, and returns just in time to meet the next tooth, thus being blocked. From the rotation speed and distance, Fizeau calculated the speed of light to be about 313,000 km/s, about 5% off from today. The experiment was conducted between two hills in the suburbs of Paris. This was the first time the speed of light was measured without using astronomy.

cau_hoi: The Chinese scholar Shen Kuo in his book "Dream Pool Essays" (around 1088) recorded what about the magnetic needle?
C: The compass needle does not point exactly to true north but is slightly off, known as magnetic declination
D: The compass needle only works at night
giai_thich: This is the earliest known record of the magnetic compass used for navigation and about magnetic declination, the angle between magnetic north and true north. In Europe, magnetic declination was only clearly recorded in the 15th century. Shen Kuo was a polymath: he wrote about astronomy, geology, medicine, and even movable type printing. Today, magnetic declination changes with location and over time, as the Earth's magnetic poles continuously move.

cau_hoi: According to Einstein's theory of special relativity, what happens to the time of an object moving at a speed very close to the speed of light?
B: Time passes slower compared to a stationary observer
C: Time completely stops at all speeds
giai_thich: This phenomenon is called "time dilation." Muons produced in the upper atmosphere only "live" for about 2 microseconds, and most would decay before reaching the ground. However, because they travel close to the speed of light, their time slows down, allowing many muons to reach the ground. In 1971, scientists took atomic clocks around the world and measured the difference exactly as predicted.

cau_hoi: Why must the GPS system adjust the clocks on satellites according to Einstein's theory of relativity?
A: Because the satellites are too cold
B: Because the satellites rotate in the opposite direction
C: If not adjusted, the satellite clocks drift about 38 microseconds each day, causing positional errors to increase by about 10 km each day
D: Because the satellites have no batteries
giai_thich: GPS satellites travel at about 14,000 km/h, so their clocks slow down by about 7 microseconds each day according to special relativity. However, at an altitude of about 20,000 km, gravity is weaker, so the clocks run faster by about 45 microseconds each day according to general relativity. The total is a net gain of about 38 microseconds. It may seem small, but light travels about 11 km in that time.

cau_hoi: What does Einstein's general theory of relativity (1915) describe gravity as?
D: The curvature of space-time caused by mass and energy
giai_thich: Imagine a stretched sheet with a bowling ball in the center causing it to sag; a marble rolling nearby will follow the curve around the bowling ball. The Sun curves space-time, and the Earth moves along the "straightest" path possible in that curved space. Physicist John Wheeler summarized: "Matter tells space-time how to curve; space-time tells matter how to move."

cau_hoi: In 1919, what phenomenon did Arthur Eddington's expedition observe during a total solar eclipse to verify the general theory of relativity?
A: The light from stars near the Sun was bent, just as Einstein predicted
giai_thich: Normally, stars near the Sun cannot be seen because they are too bright, but during a total solar eclipse, they can be. Observers on the island of Príncipe (Africa) and Sobral (Brazil) took photographs and found the positions of stars were bent by about 1.75 arc seconds, double the value predicted by Newton's theory. Newspapers worldwide reported this, and Einstein suddenly became the most famous person on the planet.

cau_hoi: In 2015, what did the LIGO detectors in the U.S. first directly detect, leading to three scientists receiving the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2017?
C: Gravitational waves from the merger of two black holes approximately 1.3 billion light-years away
giai_thich: Einstein predicted gravitational waves in 1916 but thought they were too weak to measure. LIGO used lasers running through two 4 km long tubes at right angles to each other and detected changes in length smaller than one-thousandth of a proton's diameter. The signal arrived on September 14, 2015. The Nobel Prize was awarded to Rainer Weiss, Kip Thorne, and Barry Barish. Since then, hundreds of gravitational wave events have been detected.

cau_hoi: What does the uncertainty principle proposed by Werner Heisenberg in 1927 state?
D: It is impossible to know both the exact position and momentum of a particle simultaneously
giai_thich: This is not due to poor measuring instruments, but rather the nature of the quantum world: the more precisely a particle's position is determined, the more uncertain its momentum becomes, and vice versa. For large objects like a ball, the uncertainty is so small that it is negligible. Heisenberg was only 25 years old when he proposed this principle and received the Nobel Prize in 1932 for founding quantum mechanics.

cau_hoi: What was the purpose of the thought experiment "Schrödinger's cat" (1935)?
A: To measure the weight of the cat
B: To illustrate the strangeness of applying quantum mechanics to large objects: the cat appears to be both alive and dead until the box is opened
giai_thich: In the thought experiment, a cat in a sealed box with a radioactive atom that may or may not decay. According to the conventional understanding of quantum mechanics, when not observed, the atom is in a superposition state, so the cat must also be "both alive and dead." Schrödinger intended to mock this absurdity. No real cat is involved in the experiment. Today, scientists can create superposition states with increasingly larger objects.

cau_hoi: What does the Pauli exclusion principle (1925) state about electrons in an atom?
A: No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of all quantum numbers
C: Each atom has only one electron
D: Electrons always travel in identical pairs
giai_thich: Thanks to this principle, electrons must occupy different energy levels instead of crowding into the lowest energy level, creating the structure of the periodic table and the chemical properties of elements. It also explains why we cannot pass through walls and why white dwarf stars do not collapse. Wolfgang Pauli was notoriously difficult to please, and his remark "not even wrong" was directed at vague theories.

cau_hoi: In 1928, Paul Dirac wrote an equation describing the electron, leading to the prediction of what type of matter?
giai_thich: Dirac's equation has two solutions, one for ordinary electrons and one for a particle that is identical but carries a positive charge. In 1932, Carl Anderson discovered positrons in cosmic rays, just as predicted. When matter meets antimatter, both annihilate and convert entirely into energy. PET scanners in hospitals use positrons to create images. Dirac was famously taciturn, and colleagues joked that a "dirac" was defined as one word per hour.

cau_hoi: In 1932, James Chadwick discovered which particle in the atomic nucleus?
giai_thich: Neutrons are electrically neutral and have a mass nearly equal to that of protons. Rutherford predicted its existence in 1920, but because it has no charge, neutrons are very difficult to detect. Chadwick received the Nobel Prize in 1935. This discovery was extremely important because neutrons are not repelled by the nucleus, allowing them to penetrate the nucleus, paving the way for nuclear fission and nuclear energy just a few years later.

cau_hoi: In 1938 – 1939, the phenomenon of nuclear fission of uranium was discovered by Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann and explained by which female physicist?
giai_thich: Meitner was an Austrian-born Jew who had to flee from the Nazis to Sweden in 1938. During a walk in the snow with her nephew Otto Frisch, she calculated that the uranium nucleus, when hit by a neutron, split in two, releasing energy according to the formula E = mc². In 1944, only Hahn received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, a common injustice often mentioned. Element 109, meitnerium, is named after her.

cau_hoi: On December 2, 1942, the world's first nuclear reactor, Chicago Pile-1, achieved a self-sustaining chain reaction. Who led the project?
giai_thich: The reactor was built under the stands of an abandoned football field at the University of Chicago, consisting of about 400 tons of graphite, 6 tons of metallic uranium, and many tons of uranium oxide. Cadmium control rods absorbed neutrons for safety. After the success, someone reported via telephone in code: "The Italian mariner has landed in the New World." Element 100, fermium, is named after Fermi.

cau_hoi: In 1911, Dutch physicist Heike Kamerlingh Onnes discovered what phenomenon when cooling mercury down to about 4.2 K (−269°C)?
B: Superconductivity: the resistance of mercury suddenly disappeared completely
giai_thich: Onnes was the first to liquefy helium gas in 1908, allowing for extremely low temperatures. In a superconductor, electric current can flow indefinitely without loss. Superconductivity is used in MRI machines in hospitals, maglev trains, and the giant magnets of particle accelerators. Scientists are still searching for superconducting materials at room temperature, a goal considered the "holy grail" of materials physics.

cau_hoi: What material was used to create the world's first operational laser by Theodore Maiman in 1960?
giai_thich: Laser is an acronym for "light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation," a concept originating from Einstein's paper in 1917. Maiman's laser emitted pulses of red light. At that time, some called the laser "a solution looking for a problem." Today, lasers are found in barcode scanners, eye surgery, fiber optics, printers, metal cutting, and even measuring the distance between Earth and the Moon.

cau_hoi: In 1947, where was the first transistor created by scientists John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley?
giai_thich: A transistor is a tiny semiconductor "switch" that replaced large, hot, and fragile vacuum tubes. The three won the Nobel Prize in 1956. Today, a phone chip contains tens of billions of transistors, each smaller than a virus. John Bardeen is the only person to have won the Nobel Prize in Physics twice, the second time in 1972 for explaining superconductivity.

cau_hoi: In 2012, which accelerator did scientists at CERN announce the discovery of the Higgs boson?
D: Large Hadron Collider (LHC), a circular tunnel about 27 km underground
giai_thich: The LHC is located about 100 m below the France-Switzerland border, near Geneva, accelerating protons to nearly the speed of light and colliding them. The Higgs boson is related to the mechanism that gives fundamental particles mass, predicted by Peter Higgs and many other physicists since 1964. Higgs and François Englert received the Nobel Prize in 2013. The superconducting magnets of the LHC are cooled to about −271°C, colder than outer space.

cau_hoi: What characteristic of the neutrino, predicted by Wolfgang Pauli in 1930, leads to it being called a "ghost particle"?
D: Almost does not interact with matter, with trillions of particles passing through our bodies every second without leaving a trace
giai_thich: The Sun emits a huge amount of neutrinos; about 65 billion neutrinos pass through each cm² of our bodies every second, even at night as they pass through the Earth. Pauli once worried that he had predicted a particle that would never be detected. In 1956, Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines detected neutrinos from a nuclear reactor. Neutrino detectors are often placed deep underground or in ice in Antarctica.

cau_hoi: What is the Solvay Conference in Brussels in 1927 famous for?
B: A group photo with 29 people, 17 of whom had or would win Nobel Prizes, where Einstein and Bohr debated quantum mechanics
giai_thich: The photo includes Einstein, Bohr, Marie Curie (the only woman), Planck, Heisenberg, Schrödinger, Dirac, Pauli... Here, Einstein continuously proposed thought experiments to refute the randomness of quantum mechanics, with the famous quote "God does not play dice," and Bohr is said to have replied: "Einstein, don't tell God what to do." The debate between the two lasted a lifetime.

cau_hoi: Marie Curie was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes in two different scientific fields. What were those fields?
giai_thich: In 1903, she shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with her husband Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel for their research on radioactivity. In 1911, she received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry alone for discovering polonium and radium. Polonium was named after Poland, her homeland, which at that time was not on the map due to partitioning. To this day, her notebooks are still radioactive and are kept in a lead box.

cau_hoi: In 1995, Eric Cornell and Carl Wieman first created which state of matter in the laboratory, predicted by Einstein and Indian physicist Satyendra Nath Bose in the 1920s?
giai_thich: By cooling a few thousand rubidium atoms down to just about 170 billionths of a degree above absolute zero, they "merged" into a single quantum state, like a "super atom." Bose sent a paper to Einstein in 1924 after being rejected by a journal, and Einstein translated it into German and submitted it. The boson particle, like the Higgs boson, is named after Bose. Cornell, Wieman, and Wolfgang Ketterle received the Nobel Prize in 2001.

cau_hoi: The Nobel Prize in Physics 2022 was awarded to Alain Aspect, John Clauser, and Anton Zeilinger for their experiments on which phenomenon?
B: Quantum entanglement: two particles linked together that remain correlated regardless of distance, which classical physics cannot explain
giai_thich: Einstein once referred to quantum entanglement as "spooky action at a distance" and was skeptical of it. In 1964, John Bell proposed a way to test it. The experiments of the three scientists showed that the quantum world is indeed as "strange" as quantum mechanics predicts. In 2017, a Chinese team used the Micius satellite to distribute entangled photon pairs over distances greater than 1,200 km. Quantum entanglement is the foundation for quantum computing and quantum cryptography.

cau_hoi: The Nobel Prize in Physics 2024 surprised many when it was awarded to John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton for which contribution?
D: Laying the groundwork for machine learning using artificial neural networks, based on ideas from physics
giai_thich: The Hopfield network (1982) stores and reconstructs images similarly to how physical systems of magnetic atoms find their lowest energy states. Hinton used ideas from statistical physics to build the "Boltzmann machine." These works are foundational for today's artificial intelligence, such as image recognition and chatbots. Hinton, known as the "father of AI," also warns about the risks of artificial intelligence.

cau_hoi: How was the definition of the kilogram changed in 2019?
A: Based on the mass of 1 liter of milk
C: Based on a natural constant (Planck constant) instead of a metal block kept in France
D: Based on the weight of an adult
giai_thich: Since 1889, the kilogram was defined by "Le Grand K," a platinum-iridium cylinder stored in three layers of glass bells in Sèvres, near Paris. However, copies in many countries gradually deviated by several tens of micrograms from the original. From May 20, 2019, the kilogram is defined through the Planck constant, measured by a "Kibble balance." This allows anyone, anywhere, to recreate the kilogram standard without needing to go to France.

cau_hoi: The Nobel Prize in Physics 2023 was awarded to Pierre Agostini, Ferenc Krausz, and Anne L'Huillier for creating light pulses of what duration?
giai_thich: An attosecond is 10⁻¹⁸ seconds. The number of attoseconds in one second is roughly equal to the number of seconds since the universe was born about 13.8 billion years ago. These ultrashort pulses act like extremely fast "flashes" that help capture the movement of electrons within atoms and molecules. Anne L'Huillier is the fifth woman in history to win the Nobel Prize in Physics.

cau_hoi: The Nobel Prize in Physics 2025 was awarded to John Clarke, Michel Devoret, and John Martinis for which experiment?
C: Demonstrating quantum tunneling and quantum energy in a sufficiently large circuit to hold in hand
giai_thich: In 1984-1985, the three scientists used a superconducting circuit containing Josephson junctions and showed that the entire system, consisting of billions of electrons working together, could "tunnel" through energy barriers like a quantum particle. Previously, quantum effects were mainly observed at the atomic level. This experiment is foundational for superconducting qubits in today's quantum computers; Martinis once led Google's quantum computing team.

cau_hoi: Since 1983, how has the meter been defined?
A: One ten-millionth of the distance from the equator to the North Pole
B: The distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 seconds
C: The length of a king's footstep
D: The length of a metal bar in Paris
giai_thich: In 1791, France defined the meter as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator through Paris. Two astronomers, Delambre and Méchain, took seven years to measure the meridian from Dunkirk to Barcelona during the French Revolution. The meter was then kept by a platinum-iridium bar. Since the speed of light is fixed precisely, the meter can now be recreated in any laboratory.

cau_hoi: Since 1967, a second has been defined based on what?
A: The oscillation of cesium-133 atoms, with 9,192,631,770 cycles
B: The time it takes for a grain of sand to fall
D: The time it takes for the Earth to rotate divided by 86,400
giai_thich: Previously, the second was defined by the rotation of the Earth, but the Earth's rotation is irregular, gradually slowing down due to the Moon's tidal forces. Cesium atomic clocks are accurate to about one second after tens of millions of years. New optical clocks are even more precise, capable of detecting time differences when the clock is raised just a few centimeters, according to general relativity.

cau_hoi: Which Vietnamese physicist received the Dirac Medal in 2018 and the MacArthur "Genius" Fellowship in 2018 for theoretical physics research?
giai_thich: Dam Thanh Son was born in 1968 in Hanoi and won a gold medal at the International Mathematical Olympiad in 1984. He is a professor at the University of Chicago, known for his research on matter under extreme conditions such as quark-gluon plasma, electron systems in materials, and the relationship between string theory and fluids. Ngo Bao Chau is a mathematician who won the Fields Medal in 2010, while Pham Tuan is Vietnam's first astronaut.

cau_hoi: Professor Tran Thanh Van, a Vietnamese physicist in France, is famous for which activity?
B: Founding the "Vietnam Meeting" conference series and the International Center for Interdisciplinary Science and Education (ICISE) in Quy Nhon
giai_thich: Since the 1960s, he has organized the international physics conference "Rencontres de Moriond" in France, and since 1993, the "Vietnam Meeting" has brought leading scientists from around the world, including many Nobel laureates, to Vietnam. ICISE in Quy Nhon was inaugurated in 2013. He and his wife, Professor Le Kim Ngoc, also established a fund to support poor, studious students in the country.

cau_hoi: Emmy Noether's theorem (1918) links which two concepts in physics?
C: Symmetry and conservation laws: for example, symmetry in time leads to conservation of energy
giai_thich: Noether proved that if the laws of physics do not change over time, then energy is conserved; if they do not change when shifted in space, then momentum is conserved; if they do not change when rotated, then angular momentum is conserved. She had to lecture under David Hilbert's name because the University of Göttingen did not accept female lecturers. Einstein called her one of the most creative mathematical geniuses.
