cau_hoi: After the Challenger space shuttle disaster in 1986, how did physicist Richard Feynman demonstrate the cause on television?
A: Dipped an O-ring sample into a cup of ice water and showed that it lost its elasticity when cold
D: Measured the temperature of the Sun
giai_thich: The morning of the launch in Florida was unusually cold, near freezing. The rubber O-ring became hard and could not seal the joints of the booster rocket, allowing hot gas to escape and causing the accident. Feynman used a small clamp, a cup of ice water, and a few seconds to do what many lengthy technical reports failed to clarify. He concluded: "With successful technology, reality must take precedence over public relations, for nature cannot be fooled."

cau_hoi: In 1956 – 1957, what experiment did female physicist Chien-Shiung Wu conduct that led to Yang and Lee winning the Nobel Prize?
D: Weak interaction is not mirror-symmetric: nature distinguishes left from right
giai_thich: Previously, physicists believed that all processes in nature looked exactly the same when viewed in a mirror. Yang and Lee proposed to test this in radioactive decay. Wu cooled cobalt-60 atoms near absolute zero in a magnetic field and found that electrons preferentially flew out in one direction. Yang and Lee received the Nobel Prize in 1957, while Wu was not awarded, despite being called the "first lady of physics."

cau_hoi: Hideki Yukawa, the first Japanese Nobel laureate (Physics, 1949), predicted which particle in 1935?
B: Meson, the particle that transmits the strong nuclear force holding protons and neutrons together
giai_thich: Yukawa wondered what kept positively charged protons stuck together in the nucleus despite repelling each other. He proposed a short-range strong force transmitted by a particle with an intermediate mass between the electron and proton. In 1947, the pion was discovered in cosmic rays, confirming his prediction. The 1949 Nobel Prize brought great pride to Japan after the war.

cau_hoi: Indian physicist C. V. Raman discovered which effect in 1928, making him the first Asian to win a Nobel Prize in science?
D: Light scattering through a substance can change wavelength, creating a characteristic signature of a molecule
giai_thich: According to legend, Raman became curious about the blue color of the sea while traveling to Europe in 1921. The Raman effect is now used to identify counterfeit drugs, analyze gemstones, ancient paintings, and even minerals on Mars by the Perseverance rover. India chose February 28, the day he announced his discovery, as National Science Day. He received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930.

cau_hoi: What is the blue light emitted in the water of nuclear reactors called?
giai_thich: Light travels in water slower than in a vacuum by about 25%. Charged particles like electrons can move faster than the speed of light in water (though still slower than the speed of light in a vacuum), creating a "sonic boom" of blue light. Soviet physicist Pavel Cherenkov discovered the phenomenon in 1934 and received the Nobel Prize in 1958. Huge neutrino detectors like Super-Kamiokande in Japan use this very light.

cau_hoi: "Mpemba effect," named after a Tanzanian student in 1963, describes what controversial phenomenon?
A: Under certain conditions, hot water can freeze faster than cold water
C: Ice warms up when placed in the refrigerator
D: Cold water always boils before hot water
giai_thich: Erasto Mpemba noticed that his hot ice cream mixture froze faster than his friend's when making ice cream at school. The teacher did not believe him, but later he and Professor Denis Osborne published a paper in 1969. Aristotle, Francis Bacon, and Descartes had mentioned similar phenomena. To this day, scientists still debate whether the effect is real and whether it is caused by evaporation, convection, dissolved gases, or supercooling.

cau_hoi: When shaking a box of mixed nuts, larger particles like cashews and Brazil nuts tend to rise to the top. What is this phenomenon called?
giai_thich: When shaken, smaller particles can slip down through the gaps beneath the larger particles, gradually pushing the larger particles up. There is also a convection flow of particles in the box. This phenomenon poses challenges for pharmaceutical and food factories because mixed powders can easily separate during transport. It also explains why large rocks often rise to the surface of fields after many freezing seasons in cold regions.

cau_hoi: It is said that water in sinks always swirls in opposite directions in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres due to the Coriolis force. Is this true?
C: Not true for small sinks: the Coriolis force is too weak, and the direction of the swirl is mainly due to the shape of the sink and the initial motion of the water
giai_thich: The Coriolis force due to the Earth's rotation is only significant with large, long-lasting movements like storms and ocean currents: storms in the Northern Hemisphere swirl counterclockwise, while in the Southern Hemisphere they swirl clockwise. In sinks, small differences in how water is poured have a much stronger effect. In extremely careful experiments, scientists could only measure the Coriolis effect when water was left still for many days in a large symmetrical sink.

cau_hoi: The famous free kick by Brazilian player Roberto Carlos in 1997, where the ball curved spectacularly into the net, is an example of which physical effect?
A: Magnus effect: the spinning ball creates a pressure difference on either side, causing it to bend
giai_thich: When the ball spins, one side of the surface moves in the same direction as the airflow, while the other side moves against it, creating a lateral force. German physicist Heinrich Gustav Magnus explained this in 1852, and Isaac Newton observed this phenomenon with a tennis ball as early as 1672. Studies show that Carlos's kick followed a spiral path because the ball slowed down, increasing the curvature. Baseball and table tennis players also use this effect.

cau_hoi: What strange property does a mixture of cornstarch and water (oobleck) have?
B: When struck hard, it becomes solid like a solid, but when left still or stirred gently, it flows like a liquid
giai_thich: This is a non-Newtonian fluid, with viscosity changing based on the applied force. When impacted quickly, the starch particles are pressed tightly together and cannot slide past each other, causing the mixture to harden. One can run on a pool of oobleck without sinking, but if standing still, one will gradually sink. Quicksand has a similar property: the more one struggles, the harder it is to escape, so one must move slowly.

cau_hoi: What is the triple point of water?
A: The unique temperature and pressure at which water can exist simultaneously in all three phases: solid, liquid, and gas in equilibrium
B: The freezing point of water at three degrees
D: Three times the boiling point of water
giai_thich: The triple point of water occurs at about 0.01°C and a pressure of about 611 Pa, which is only about 0.6% of atmospheric pressure. Under these conditions, water can boil and freeze at the same time. From 1954 to 2019, the triple point of water was used to define the kelvin unit. On Mars, the surface pressure is close to the triple point pressure, making it difficult for liquid water to exist for long; it easily freezes or evaporates.

cau_hoi: What happens when a piece of iron magnet is heated beyond about 770°C?
B: It loses its magnetism, as it has surpassed the Curie temperature
giai_thich: In a magnet, small "magnetic domains" are aligned in the same direction. High temperatures cause the atoms to vibrate strongly, disrupting that alignment. Pierre Curie studied this phenomenon in 1895, before researching radioactivity with his wife. When volcanic rock cools below the Curie temperature, iron minerals "record" the Earth's magnetic field direction at that time, helping geologists discover that the Earth's magnetic field has reversed many times.

cau_hoi: Where do the Voyager space probes, flying far from the Sun where solar panels are ineffective, get their power from?
D: Radioisotope thermoelectric generators: heat from plutonium-238 decay is converted into electricity via the Seebeck effect
giai_thich: In 1821, Thomas Seebeck discovered that when two different metals are connected and kept at different temperatures, an electric current appears. RTGs have no moving parts, making them very durable. Launched in 1977, Voyager still sends signals back nearly 50 years later, despite gradually decreasing power of about 4 W per year, forcing engineers to sequentially turn off equipment. The Curiosity and Perseverance rovers on Mars also use RTGs.

cau_hoi: What physical effect do quartz watches operate on, discovered by brothers Pierre and Jacques Curie in 1880?
C: Piezoelectric effect: quartz crystals generate voltage when compressed and vibrate steadily when voltage is applied
giai_thich: The quartz crystal in the watch is cut into the shape of a small tuning fork, vibrating precisely 32,768 times per second, or 2¹⁵, making it easy for the circuit to divide by 15 to produce exactly one pulse per second. The first quartz watch was sold in 1969 by Seiko (Japan). The piezoelectric effect is also found in gas lighters, tiny speakers, ultrasound machines, and vibration sensors.

cau_hoi: What did glassmaker Joseph von Fraunhofer discover in 1814 while observing the solar spectrum?
A: Hundreds of dark lines in the color spectrum, later known to be caused by elements in the Sun's atmosphere absorbing light
giai_thich: Fraunhofer was an orphan who was buried in a glass factory collapse, rescued and funded by the prince of Bavaria. He made high-quality prisms and spectroscopes, recording over 570 dark lines. In 1859, Kirchhoff and Bunsen explained that each element absorbs specific colors. The element helium was discovered in the Sun through the spectrum in 1868, before being found on Earth.

cau_hoi: What formula is inscribed on the tombstone of Austrian physicist Ludwig Boltzmann in Vienna?
D: S = k log W, relating entropy to the number of microstates of the system
giai_thich: Boltzmann pointed out that entropy, the degree of "disorder", actually measures the number of ways atoms can be arranged while still yielding the same observable state. Disordered states have many more arrangements than ordered states, so nature tends to move towards disorder. In his time, many scientists did not even believe in the existence of atoms and vehemently opposed him. Boltzmann's constant k is one of the constants used to define the kelvin unit since 2019.

cau_hoi: "Maxwell's Demon" (1867) is a thought experiment that challenges which law?
C: Second law of thermodynamics, when a small being sorts fast and slow molecules to create a temperature difference without expending work
giai_thich: "The demon" stands at a small door between two gas chambers, only allowing fast molecules to pass to one side and slow molecules to the other, making one side hot and the other cold, seemingly reducing entropy. This problem puzzled physicists for over 100 years. The solution was provided by Rolf Landauer and Charles Bennett: the demon must store and erase information about the molecules, and the act of erasing information always releases heat, so the law still holds.

cau_hoi: In 1912, Austrian physicist Victor Hess flew a balloon to an altitude of about 5 km and discovered what?
B: Ionizing radiation increases with altitude, proving that there are "cosmic rays" coming from outer space
D: The air at high altitudes is warmer
giai_thich: Previously, it was thought that radiation in the air came from radioactive rocks in the Earth's crust, so it should decrease with altitude. Hess flew both during the day and during a solar eclipse, observing that radiation did not decrease, concluding that the source was not the Sun. Cosmic rays are high-energy particles, mostly protons, coming from distant stellar explosions. Hess won the Nobel Prize in 1936.

cau_hoi: What quantity did Robert Millikan's "oil drop" experiment (1909) measure?
giai_thich: Millikan sprayed tiny oil droplets between two charged metal plates, then adjusted the electric field to keep the droplets suspended against gravity. He found that the charge of the droplets was always an integer multiple of a smallest value, about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs, which is the charge of an electron. Millikan won the Nobel Prize in 1923. Later, his data selection in the records caused some controversy.

cau_hoi: The cloud chamber invented by Scottish physicist Charles Wilson in 1911 helps scientists do what?
B: See the paths of subatomic particles through condensed water vapor trails, similar to airplane smoke trails
giai_thich: Wilson was inspired while observing optical phenomena on Ben Nevis and wanted to create clouds in the laboratory. When charged particles pass through saturated water vapor, they leave behind thin mist trails. Thanks to the cloud chamber, Carl Anderson discovered positrons in 1932. Today, students can make simple cloud chambers using plastic boxes, alcohol, and dry ice to observe cosmic rays.

cau_hoi: In 1924, what bold idea did Louis de Broglie propose in his doctoral thesis?
B: Atoms are as large as grains of sand
D: Not only light but also particles of matter like electrons have wave properties
giai_thich: De Broglie, from a French noble family and initially studying history, argued that if light waves have particle properties, then particles must also have wave properties. The thesis committee was uncertain and sent it to Einstein for review; Einstein was very supportive. In 1927, Davisson and Germer in the U.S. observed electrons diffracting on a nickel crystal like waves. De Broglie received the Nobel Prize in 1929. Electron microscopes are based on the wave properties of electrons.

cau_hoi: In 1989, what famous achievement did IBM scientists accomplish using a scanning tunneling microscope?
B: Measuring the temperature of the Sun
giai_thich: The scanning tunneling microscope (STM) was invented by Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer in 1981 at IBM Zurich, using a sharp tip with only one atom at its end. The quantum tunneling current between the tip and the surface allows for "seeing" individual atoms. The two received the Nobel Prize in 1986. In 2013, IBM also created the world's smallest animation "The Boy and His Atom" by moving individual atoms.

cau_hoi: In 2004, how did Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov isolate graphene, a material just one atom thick, using a simple tool?
D: Tape, peeling multiple times from a piece of graphite
giai_thich: They conducted this experiment during "Friday night experiments," where they freely tried out crazy ideas. Graphene is about 200 times stronger than steel, has excellent electrical and thermal conductivity, and is nearly transparent. The two received the Nobel Prize in 2010. Previously, in 2000, Geim received the Ig Nobel Prize for making a live frog levitate using a strong magnetic field. He is the only person to have received both awards.

cau_hoi: What causes the "wet road" illusion seen from afar on asphalt on hot days?
C: A layer of hot air close to the road bends light from the sky, creating an image like a water reflection
giai_thich: Hot air has a lower refractive index than cold air. Light from the sky, when it encounters the hot air layer, is gradually refracted and bends back up to the observer's eyes, making the brain think there is a "puddle" reflecting the sky. This is an "under" illusion. In cold sea areas, light can bend downwards, creating an "above" illusion, like boats floating in the sky, known as Fata Morgana.

cau_hoi: Why do polarized sunglasses reduce glare from water and roads more effectively than regular sunglasses?
A: Reflected light from horizontal surfaces is mostly polarized horizontally, and the glasses block that oscillation direction
D: The lenses are made of diamond
giai_thich: Light is a wave oscillating in many directions. When reflected on water, horizontally oscillating light predominates. Polarized glasses only allow vertically oscillating light to pass through, thus blocking most of the glare. Fishermen use this type of glasses to see fish beneath the water's surface. If you tilt your head while looking at a phone screen through polarized glasses, the screen can appear completely dark.

cau_hoi: Why does inhaling helium make your voice high-pitched and squeaky like a cartoon character?
B: Sound travels in helium about 3 times faster than in air, changing the resonant frequency of the mouth and throat
giai_thich: The vocal cords still vibrate at nearly the same frequency, but the mouth and throat act as a resonating chamber. When sound travels faster, the resonant frequencies increase, making the pitch sound higher. Conversely, the heavy gas sulfur hexafluoride makes the voice much deeper. Note: inhaling helium should not be done as it can cause dangerous oxygen deprivation, especially when inhaled directly from a pressurized tank.

cau_hoi: In 2012, Felix Baumgartner jumped from an altitude of about 39 km in the stratosphere and set what record?
A: The highest person to fly by airplane
B: The first person to break the sound barrier in free fall without a vehicle
C: The first person to go to the Moon
giai_thich: The air at that altitude is very thin, so the drag is small, allowing Baumgartner to reach speeds of about 1,358 km/h. As he descended, denser air slowed him down before he deployed his parachute at an altitude of about 1.5 km. Over 8 million people watched live on YouTube. In 2014, Alan Eustace jumped from an altitude of about 41 km, breaking Baumgartner's altitude record.

cau_hoi: Why do neon gas advertising lights emit a characteristic orange-red light?
A: Electric current excites neon atoms, and when electrons return to a lower energy level, they emit light with a characteristic wavelength of neon
B: The glass tube is painted red
giai_thich: Each gas has its own "color signature": neon is orange-red, helium is light pink, argon is light blue, and sodium vapor is yellow-orange like old streetlights. Many "neon" blue lights actually use argon gas with a bit of mercury and a phosphorescent coating. Chemist Georges Claude demonstrated neon lights in Paris in 1910. Neon was discovered by William Ramsay and Morris Travers in 1898, and its name comes from the Greek word meaning "new".

cau_hoi: In 1964, Murray Gell-Mann and George Zweig independently proposed that protons and neutrons are made up of smaller particles. Where did Gell-Mann get the name "quark" from?
B: From the name of a city
C: From a line in the novel "Finnegans Wake" by James Joyce
D: From the name of a bird
giai_thich: The line "Three quarks for Muster Mark!" fits with the idea that protons consist of three quarks. There are six types of quarks: up, down, strange, charm, bottom, and top. A proton consists of two up quarks and one down quark. Quarks never exist alone; they are always "trapped" in larger particles by the strong force. Gell-Mann received the Nobel Prize in 1969.

cau_hoi: Where and how heavy was the heaviest quark, the top quark, discovered in 1995?
A: In Japan; it has no mass
B: On the Moon; as heavy as a grain of sand
C: At CERN; lighter than an electron
D: At Fermilab (USA); nearly as heavy as a gold atom
giai_thich: The top quark weighs about 173 GeV, more than 180 times that of a proton. It decays so quickly that it cannot combine with another quark, only about 5 × 10⁻²⁵ seconds. Scientists had to collide protons with antiprotons at the Tevatron accelerator, which is about 6.3 km long, to create it. The discovery of the top quark completed the set of six quarks predicted by the Standard Model.

cau_hoi: The Nobel Prize in Physics in 1965 was awarded to Richard Feynman, Julian Schwinger, and Shin'ichirō Tomonaga for developing which theory?
A: Quantum Electrodynamics (QED), the most accurately tested theory ever
giai_thich: QED describes how light and matter interact. Its prediction of the electron's magnetic moment matches experiments to about 12 decimal places, akin to measuring the distance from New York to Los Angeles accurate to the thickness of a hair. Feynman devised simple 'Feynman diagrams' to represent complex calculations, now used throughout particle physics. Tomonaga worked independently in Japan during wartime.

cau_hoi: In 1923, Arthur Compton discovered that X-rays scattered off electrons had increased wavelengths. What does this prove?
C: Light consists of photons with momentum, colliding like billiard balls
giai_thich: Before Compton, many physicists were skeptical of Einstein's photon idea. Compton showed that X-rays collide with electrons like two billiard balls: photons lose some energy, thus their wavelengths increase, in accordance with the conservation of energy and momentum. Compton won the Nobel Prize in 1927. NASA's Compton Gamma Ray Observatory (1991 – 2000) is named after him.

cau_hoi: In 1901, Ernest Rutherford and Frederick Soddy discovered what 'resembled alchemy' about the element thorium?
B: Thorium turns into gold when heated
D: The radioactive element spontaneously transforms into another element
giai_thich: Upon realizing thorium was spontaneously transforming into another gas, Soddy exclaimed: 'Rutherford, this is elemental transmutation!', to which Rutherford replied: 'Don't call it transmutation, they'll chop our heads off like alchemists.' They also introduced the concept of half-life. Rutherford won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1908, joking that he had witnessed many transformations, but the quickest was his own change from physicist to chemist.

cau_hoi: In 1879, graduate student Edwin Hall discovered what phenomenon, now used in wheel speed sensors and phone compasses?
B: When a current-carrying conductor is placed in a magnetic field, a small voltage appears perpendicular to the direction of the current
giai_thich: Electrons moving in a magnetic field are deflected by the Lorentz force to one side of the conductor, creating a charge difference at the edges. Hall sensors are used in phones for compasses, in keyboards, drives, and even motorcycles and cars. A century later, in 1980, Klaus von Klitzing discovered the 'quantum Hall effect' at very low temperatures, with resistance values so precise they are used as a measurement standard.

cau_hoi: American scientist Joseph Henry, contemporary of Faraday, is famous for which invention, and which unit is named after him?
B: Very strong electromagnet and self-induction phenomenon; henry unit
giai_thich: Henry wound hundreds of turns of insulated wire around an iron core, creating an electromagnet that could lift over a ton. He independently discovered electromagnetic induction around the same time as Faraday, but published later. Henry also created a long-wire electric bell system, contributing to the telegraph idea. He was the first director of the Smithsonian Institution (USA) from 1846.

cau_hoi: In 1839, at just 19 years old, Edmond Becquerel (father of Henri Becquerel) discovered which phenomenon?
C: The photovoltaic effect in batteries: light shining on electrodes generates current, the foundation of solar panels
giai_thich: He placed two electrodes in an electrolyte solution and observed that the current increased when illuminated. In 1883, Charles Fritts created the first solar cell using gold-coated selenium, with an efficiency of about 1%. In 1954, Bell Labs produced the first practical silicon solar cell, with an efficiency of about 6%. Today, commercially available solar panels achieve efficiencies of around 20-23%. The Becquerel family has four generations of physicists.

cau_hoi: The Geiger counter, a device that makes a 'clicking' sound when detecting radiation, was developed by Hans Geiger along with whom into its modern form in 1928?
giai_thich: The tube contains gas at low pressure and has a high voltage between the two electrodes. When a radioactive particle passes through, it ionizes the gas, creating an 'avalanche' of electrons into an electric pulse, which is converted into a clicking sound. Geiger was previously Rutherford's assistant in the gold foil experiment. The 1928 version was much more sensitive and durable, hence the device is commonly referred to as the Geiger-Müller counter.

cau_hoi: "The green flash" sometimes seen for a few seconds right as the Sun sets below the horizon is caused by what?
A: The atmosphere refracting light strongly, causing the green light to bend more and appear last at the top edge of the Sun
giai_thich: The atmosphere acts like a weak prism, slightly separating the Sun's image into overlapping colors. Blue and violet are scattered almost entirely, so green is the last color visible at the top edge. The phenomenon requires a distant horizon, clear and stable air. The writer Jules Verne even wrote a novel titled 'The Green Ray' (1882) about people searching for this phenomenon.

cau_hoi: German physicist Ernst Chladni (18th century) conducted which famous experiment with sand and metal plates?
A: Heating the plate until it glows red
B: Sprinkling sand on the plate and drawing a violin bow along the edge, causing the sand to gather into beautiful patterns at the nodes
giai_thich: When the plate vibrates at a resonant frequency, there are areas of strong vibration and completely still lines called nodal lines. The sand is thrown off the vibrating areas and settles at the nodal lines, creating 'Chladni figures'. Napoleon was very impressed and offered a prize to anyone who could mathematically explain it; female mathematician Sophie Germain won the prize in 1816. Violin makers use this technique to test the plates.

cau_hoi: According to legend, what did Pythagoras discover about music while studying string instruments?
A: Strings must be made of gold
D: Harmonic intervals correspond to simple ratios of string lengths, such as 1:2 for an octave
giai_thich: Plucking a string and then pressing it in the middle produces a sound that is exactly one octave higher. The ratio of 2:3 gives a perfect fifth, and 3:4 gives a perfect fourth. This is one of the earliest examples of using mathematics to describe nature. Today we know that the frequency of sound is inversely proportional to the length of the string and depends on tension and mass. The tighter and thinner the string, the higher the pitch.

cau_hoi: When blowing across the mouth of an empty bottle, we hear a sound like "u u". How does the sound change when blowing into a bottle with more water?
C: Higher pitch, because the air volume in the bottle is smaller
giai_thich: The bottle acts as a Helmholtz resonator, studied by Hermann von Helmholtz in the 19th century: the air mass in the neck of the bottle oscillates up and down like a weight on a spring, while the air mass in the body of the bottle acts as the "spring". The smaller the air volume, the stiffer the "spring" and the higher the frequency. Note: if you tap the bottle, the opposite occurs; a bottle with more water produces a lower sound because the water mass causes the bottle to oscillate more slowly.

cau_hoi: In 1997, what record did the Thrust SSC car, driven by Andy Green, set in the Black Rock Desert (USA)?
A: The first ground vehicle to officially exceed the speed of sound, approximately 1,228 km/h
B: The vehicle that traveled the farthest on one liter of gasoline
D: The smallest car in the world
giai_thich: The Thrust SSC uses two jet engines from fighter planes, with a power equivalent to about 1,000 family cars. The record was set on October 15, 1997, exactly 50 years and one day after Chuck Yeager first flew faster than the speed of sound. The supersonic boom of the car kicked up dust across the desert. Andy Green is a pilot of the Royal Air Force.

cau_hoi: Fighter pilots can experience an acceleration of about 9g when making sharp turns. What can happen without protective measures?
A: Blood rushes to the legs, the brain lacks blood leading to blurred vision and possible fainting
B: The pilot flies up to the ceiling
C: The pilot becomes nine times lighter
giai_thich: At 9g, the body weighs nine times its normal weight, making it difficult for the heart to pump blood to the brain. First, the pilot loses color, then vision narrows as if looking through a tube ("tunnel vision"), and may eventually faint. Pilots wear g-suits with air bladders that compress their legs and abdomen, while also performing muscle tensing and special breathing techniques. They are trained in a centrifuge.

cau_hoi: Astronauts on the International Space Station (about 400 km high) are floating. How does the gravitational force there compare to that on Earth?
B: Still about 90%; they float because both the station and the people are continuously "falling" around the Earth
giai_thich: The space station travels at a speed of about 28,000 km/h horizontally. It is always falling towards the Earth, but because it is moving horizontally fast enough, the surface of the Earth curves away, so the station never touches the ground. Everything on the station falls together, creating a sensation of weightlessness, similar to the feeling of free fall when an elevator suddenly descends. Newton described this idea with the image of a cannon firing a projectile from the top of a mountain.

cau_hoi: When a skydiver is in free fall in a prone position, what is the maximum speed (terminal velocity) approximately?
giai_thich: As the speed increases, air resistance increases significantly until it equals the person's weight, at which point speed no longer increases. If the diver points their head down, the cross-sectional area is smaller, allowing the skydiver to reach speeds of about 300 km/h or more. Small, light objects like raindrops have a low terminal velocity, around 30 km/h, so rain does not injure us. Small insects falling from a height usually survive because the air resistance is very large compared to their weight.

cau_hoi: The 2018 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Arthur Ashkin for "optical tweezers" and to Gérard Mourou and Donna Strickland for what technique?
C: Chirp pulse amplification, creating extremely powerful and ultra-short laser pulses used in eye surgery
giai_thich: Optical tweezers use a focused laser beam to hold and move extremely small objects like bacteria and cells without touching them. Ashkin received the award at the age of 96, making him the oldest Nobel laureate at that time. Strickland and Mourou extended laser pulses, amplified them, and then compressed them, creating extremely powerful pulses without damaging the equipment. Strickland is the third woman to win the Nobel Prize in Physics, after Marie Curie (1903) and Maria Goeppert Mayer (1963).

cau_hoi: The 2021 Nobel Prize in Physics honored climate research for the first time. Syukuro Manabe and Klaus Hasselmann were awarded for what?
C: Measuring the temperature of the Moon
D: Building a physical model of Earth's climate, reliably predicting global warming
giai_thich: Since the 1960s, Manabe showed that doubling CO₂ levels would raise surface temperatures by about 2°C, a prediction that remains quite accurate with modern models. Hasselmann developed a method to distinguish the "fingerprint" of human influence from natural climate variability. The other half of the prize was awarded to Giorgio Parisi for his research on complex and chaotic physical systems.

cau_hoi: In December 2022, the National Ignition Facility (NIF) in the USA achieved what historic milestone in nuclear fusion?
A: For the first time, a nuclear fusion reaction produced more energy than the energy from the laser directed at the fuel
B: Discovery of new fuel on the Moon
C: Creating an artificial Sun that powers an entire city
D: Completion of a commercial nuclear fusion power plant
giai_thich: 192 extremely powerful laser beams were directed at a fuel pellet of deuterium-tritium smaller than a peppercorn, compressing and heating it to temperatures higher than the core of the Sun. The reaction produced about 3.15 megajoules, compared to 2.05 megajoules from the laser input. However, operating the laser requires a much larger amount of electricity, so commercial nuclear fusion power is still a long way off. Nuclear fusion promises a clean energy source with minimal long-lived radioactive waste.

cau_hoi: Where is the ITER project, the world's largest experimental nuclear fusion reactor involving 35 countries, being built?
giai_thich: ITER uses a donut-shaped tokamak design to contain plasma heated to about 150 million degrees Celsius, ten times hotter than the core of the Sun, using a massive superconducting magnetic field. The goal is to produce ten times the thermal energy input to heat the plasma. The project has faced years of delays and skyrocketing costs; according to the updated 2024 plan, the first scientific experiments are expected in the mid-2030s.

cau_hoi: Why can stars generate energy by fusing light elements, but cannot continue once the core has become iron?
C: Iron nuclei have one of the highest binding energies per nucleon, so fusing to create heavier elements no longer releases energy
giai_thich: Fusing nuclei lighter than iron and fissioning heavy nuclei like uranium both release energy because the products are closer to iron. When a massive star's core turns into iron, it loses its energy source and collapses in less than a second, causing a supernova explosion. Thus, the iron in our blood was formed in the cores of massive stars that died long ago.

cau_hoi: What strange phenomenon does the Casimir effect, predicted by Hendrik Casimir in 1948, describe?
C: Two uncharged metal plates placed very close together in a vacuum still attract each other due to quantum fluctuations of the vacuum
giai_thich: According to quantum mechanics, the vacuum is not actually 'empty' but always has small energy fluctuations. Between two plates that are very close together, only some 'just right' fluctuations can fit in, fewer than outside, so the external pressure pushes the two plates closer together. The force is only significant at distances of a thousandth of a millimeter or less. In 1997, Steve Lamoreaux accurately measured this force for the first time.

cau_hoi: In 1999, Danish physicist Lene Hau slowed light down to approximately what speed while passing through a Bose-Einstein condensate?
B: About 17 m/s, slower than a racing bicycle
giai_thich: Hau's team used a supercooled sodium atomic cloud and controlled laser beams to slow light down to the point where it could be 'caught up with' by running. In 2001, the team even managed to stop light completely, storing information in atoms, and then releasing the light again. This does not violate relativity, as the speed of light in a vacuum remains the ultimate limit.

cau_hoi: In December 2024, Google announced the Willow quantum chip with 105 qubits. What did they claim about its computational capabilities?
A: Replace all computers in the world
D: Solve a test problem in about 5 minutes that the most powerful supercomputer would take about 10²⁵ years
giai_thich: The test problem 'sampling random circuits' was chosen because it is extremely difficult for classical computers, and has no practical application yet. More importantly, Willow demonstrates that as the number of qubits increases, errors decrease exponentially, a milestone in quantum error correction that scientists have pursued for nearly 30 years. Qubits can exist in a superposition state between 0 and 1, but are very susceptible to environmental noise.

cau_hoi: In 2008, Vietnam hosted the 39th International Physics Olympiad (IPhO) for the first time in which city?
giai_thich: The competition gathered over 370 students from about 80 countries and territories. The IPhO was first held in 1967 in Warsaw (Poland). The Vietnamese team has participated in the IPhO since 1982 and has won many gold medals. Each team consists of up to 5 high school students, who take two parts: theory and practical, each lasting 5 hours.

cau_hoi: In 2021, scientists in Bremen (Germany) achieved a record low effective temperature of about 38 pico kelvin by what means?
B: Using an extremely large household refrigerator
D: Dropping a supercooled atomic cloud in free fall in a 110 m drop tower and using a magnetic field to 'turn off' their motion
giai_thich: 38 pico kelvin is 38 trillionths of a degree above absolute zero. In the drop tower, the Bose-Einstein condensate atoms fall freely, not being stretched by gravity, so the scientists used a magnetic pulse as a 'lens' to nearly stop them from expanding. This record lasted about 2 seconds. Such experiments help test quantum mechanics and relativity with unprecedented accuracy.

cau_hoi: What is the highest temperature ever created by humans in a laboratory, approximately 5.5 trillion degrees Celsius, achieved?
C: In lead nuclear collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC)
giai_thich: This is about 300,000 times hotter than the center of the Sun; at this temperature, protons and neutrons 'melt' into quark-gluon plasma, a 'soup' of free quarks and gluons similar to the state of the universe a few microseconds after the Big Bang. Scientists were surprised to find that this plasma behaves like an almost perfect liquid, with the least friction ever known, rather than a gas. It only exists for an extremely short moment.

cau_hoi: In 1974, what shocking prediction did Stephen Hawking make about black holes?
B: Black holes are not completely black but emit weak radiation due to quantum effects, and can 'evaporate' over time
C: Black holes suck in the entire universe
giai_thich: According to relativity, nothing escapes from a black hole. But when combining quantum mechanics near the event horizon, Hawking calculated that black holes must have a temperature and emit radiation, now called Hawking radiation. The smaller the black hole, the hotter and faster it evaporates. For a black hole the mass of the Sun, the radiation is so weak that it cannot be measured, and the evaporation time is much longer than the age of the universe.

cau_hoi: What does the 'twin paradox' in relativity describe?
A: A person traveling into space at near-light speed and then returning will be younger than their twin sibling who stayed on Earth
B: The person who stayed on Earth is younger
giai_thich: It's called a 'paradox' because at first glance, each person could claim the other is moving. But the situation is not symmetrical: the traveler must accelerate, turn around, and decelerate, so only that person is younger. Astronaut Scott Kelly lived nearly a year on the International Space Station (2015-2016) and returned younger than his twin brother Mark by about a few milliseconds. The effect has been verified using atomic clocks.

cau_hoi: Richard Feynman's lecture 'There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom' (1959) is considered the origin of ideas for which field?
giai_thich: Feynman asked: why can't we write the entire 24-volume Encyclopedia Britannica on the head of a pin? He also offered two $1,000 prizes: for the person who could make a smaller electric motor than a cube with a side of 1/64 inch, and for the person who could shrink a page of a book 25,000 times. The first prize was awarded just a year later; the second was awarded in 1985 to a graduate student who used an electron beam to write the first page of the story 'Two Cities'.

cau_hoi: What skill does the famous 'Fermi problem' like 'How many piano tuners are in Chicago?' teach?
C: Quickly estimating difficult-to-know numbers by breaking them down into reasonable assumptions
giai_thich: For example: Chicago has about 3 million people, about 1 million households, maybe 1/20 of homes have pianos, each piano is tuned once a year, each tuner works on about 1,000 pianos a year, so there are about 50 tuners. Errors often cancel each other out, so the result is correct to the order of magnitude. Enrico Fermi was famous for this estimation skill: during the Trinity test in 1945, he dropped a piece of paper and estimated the explosion's power from the distance the paper was blown away.

cau_hoi: "Ultraviolet catastrophe" at the end of the 19th century refers to what issue that classical physics could not resolve?
A: Classical theory predicted that hot objects emit infinite energy at short wavelengths, contrary to reality
B: The Sun emits too little light
D: Ultraviolet rays destroy the ozone layer
giai_thich: According to the Rayleigh-Jeans formula based on classical physics, radiation energy increases indefinitely as wavelength decreases, meaning an oven should also emit ultraviolet and X-rays with infinite energy. Clearly, this does not happen. In 1900, Planck resolved the issue by assuming energy is quantized. The term "ultraviolet catastrophe" was coined by Paul Ehrenfest in 1911.

cau_hoi: The Stern-Gerlach experiment (1922) showed a beam of silver atoms passing through a non-uniform magnetic field separating into how many streaks on the screen?
D: Two distinct streaks, indicating a quantum quantity (spin) that only takes two values
giai_thich: According to classical physics, "atomic magnets" are randomly oriented, so they should create a continuous streak. However, the atomic beam separated neatly into two. According to legend, the silver streak on the glass plate was too faint, only becoming clear when Stern smoked a cheap cigar containing a lot of sulfur, causing the silver to turn into black silver sulfide. In 1925, Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit explained the results using the concept of electron spin.

cau_hoi: In 1896, Dutch physicist Pieter Zeeman discovered what when placing a sodium flame in a strong magnetic field?
B: The flame flew to the ceiling
D: The spectral lines split into multiple lines
giai_thich: The Zeeman effect shows that a magnetic field affects the electron energy levels in an atom. Hendrik Lorentz explained it using electron theory, and both shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1902. In 1908, astronomer George Ellery Hale used the Zeeman effect to discover sunspots with very strong magnetic fields. Today, astronomers still use it to measure the magnetic fields of distant stars.

cau_hoi: In 1935, Einstein along with Podolsky and Rosen published the "EPR" paper to argue what?
A: Quantum mechanics is incomplete, as quantum entanglement seems to allow for instantaneous influence at a distance
C: The theory of relativity is wrong
giai_thich: According to the EPR argument, if measuring one particle immediately reveals the properties of another particle far away, then those properties must have been "pre-existing", meaning there are "hidden variables" that quantum mechanics overlooks. In the same year, Schrödinger coined the term "entanglement" to describe this phenomenon. Nearly 30 years later, John Bell found a way to test it experimentally, and experiments showed that Einstein was wrong in this case.

cau_hoi: "Lamb shift" measured by Willis Lamb in 1947 has what significant meaning?
B: Two energy levels of hydrogen predicted to be equal by Dirac's theory are slightly different, paving the way for quantum electrodynamics
D: The energy levels of hydrogen remain constant in all cases
giai_thich: The difference is very small, only about one part per million of the binding energy, but was measured by Lamb and Robert Retherford using microwave techniques developed from wartime radar. The cause is the electron interacting with quantum fluctuations of the vacuum. Just days after the 1947 Shelter Island conference, Hans Bethe calculated this value accurately on a train. Lamb received the Nobel Prize in 1955.

cau_hoi: In 1962, 22-year-old graduate student Brian Josephson predicted what phenomenon, helping him win the Nobel Prize in 1973?
C: Supercurrent can flow through a thin insulating layer between two superconductors without needing a voltage
giai_thich: The Josephson effect is an example of quantum tunneling on a large scale. SQUID devices using this effect are sensitive enough to measure the magnetic fields of human brain activity. The effect is also used as a standard for measuring voltage in metrology institutes. Initially, the renowned physicist John Bardeen doubted Josephson's prediction, but the 1963 experiment confirmed it.

cau_hoi: The Meissner effect (1933) shows what special property of superconductors besides having zero resistance?
B: Completely expels magnetic fields from within, allowing a magnet to levitate above it
giai_thich: Walther Meissner and Robert Ochsenfeld discovered that magnetic fields are "expelled" from superconductors when cooled, so this is not just a perfect conductor but a new state of matter. The image of a magnet levitating above a superconducting ceramic plate evaporating liquid nitrogen is a symbol of superconductivity. Some types of maglev trains, like Japan's SCMaglev line, use superconducting magnets.

cau_hoi: The BCS theory (1957) explains superconductivity using which concept?
D: Electrons pair up into "Cooper pairs" through interactions with lattice vibrations, then move together without resistance
giai_thich: John Bardeen, Leon Cooper, and John Robert Schrieffer proposed this theory. One electron passing through causes positive ions in the crystal to slightly compress, creating a second electron attraction region, similar to two people rolling toward each other on a soft cushion. Millions of such pairs operate synchronously like a giant quantum wave. The three received the Nobel Prize in 1972, and it was Bardeen's second Nobel Prize.

cau_hoi: In 1986, Georg Bednorz and Alex Müller at IBM Zurich discovered what that sparked a surge in superconductivity research?
C: A type of high-temperature superconducting ceramic that exceeded all previous materials
giai_thich: This ceramic is superconducting at about 35 K, while theories at the time suggested a limit of around 30 K. Just a year later, YBCO ceramic was found to be superconducting at about 93 K, higher than the boiling point of liquid nitrogen (77 K), a coolant as cheap as milk. The March 1987 conference on this topic was so crowded it was dubbed the "Woodstock of Physics". The two received the Nobel Prize in 1987, just a year after the discovery.

cau_hoi: In 2023, the material LK-99 was claimed by a group in South Korea to be a room-temperature superconductor. What were the verification results?
A: Laboratories worldwide could not reproduce it; the phenomenon resembling "levitation" was due to copper sulfide impurities and magnetic properties
B: It is being used in all phones
C: It was recognized as the greatest discovery of the century
giai_thich: A video showing LK-99 slightly lifting one end above a magnet went viral on social media, and many were excited to try it themselves. Within weeks, research groups showed that resistance dropped sharply due to copper sulfide phase transition at around 104°C, not superconductivity. The incident is a lesson on how science self-corrects: extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence and must be reproducible by others.

cau_hoi: In 1937 – 1938, Pyotr Kapitsa and the team of John Allen and Don Misener independently discovered liquid helium below about 2.17 K. What strange property does it have?
B: Superfluid: flows without friction, can crawl up the walls of the container and spout out
giai_thich: Superfluid helium can flow through tiny openings that ordinary liquids cannot pass through, and forms a thin film that crawls up the walls of the container and spills out. When gently heating a tube containing fine powder submerged in superfluid helium, it creates a "fountain" that shoots up. Kapitsa received the Nobel Prize in 1978, more than 40 years after the discovery. Lev Landau explained the theory and received the Nobel Prize in 1962.

cau_hoi: The Nobel Prize in Physics 2015 was awarded to Takaaki Kajita and Arthur McDonald for what discovery about neutrinos?
A: Neutrinos oscillate, changing types as they travel, proving they have mass
giai_thich: The original Standard Model assumed neutrinos had no mass. Since the 1960s, Raymond Davis's experiment at the Homestake mine counted only about one-third of the predicted number of neutrinos from the Sun, known as the "solar neutrino problem." The Super-Kamiokande detector (Japan, 1998) and SNO (Canada, 2001) showed that neutrinos do not disappear but change "flavors" along their path. This can only happen if they have mass.

cau_hoi: In 2011, the OPERA experiment (Italy) announced that neutrinos seemed to travel faster than light. What was the cause in the end?
B: Neutrinos are indeed faster than light
C: A loose optical fiber and a misaligned clock caused timing errors
D: Light was slowed down in Italy
giai_thich: Neutrinos traveled from CERN to the Gran Sasso laboratory, about 730 km away, seemingly arriving about 60 nanoseconds early. The scientists publicly announced the results to invite others to find errors. In 2012, they discovered that a loose optical fiber connecting the GPS system to the computer caused the timing error. The team leader subsequently resigned. Physicist Jim Al-Khalili once promised to eat his shorts on television if the results were correct.

cau_hoi: The g-2 experiment on muons at Fermilab will announce its final results in 2025. What is the notable conclusion?
B: Muons are heavier than the Sun
D: The measured value is very accurate and matches new theoretical predictions based on supercomputer calculations, gradually diminishing signs of "new physics"
giai_thich: Muons are similar to electrons but about 207 times heavier. When spinning in a magnetic field, it "wobbles" at a rate dependent on all the virtual particles that briefly appear in the vacuum. From 2001 to 2021, the measured results seemed to deviate from theory, suggesting the existence of unknown particles. However, new calculations using the "lattice" method on supercomputers provided theoretical values closer to the measured results. The experiment's giant magnet was transported by ship and truck from New York to Chicago in 2013.

cau_hoi: "The proton radius puzzle" that began in 2010 is what?
C: Measuring the proton radius using hydrogen atoms with muons instead of electrons yields a result about 4% smaller than previous measurements
D: Protons are as big as a ball
giai_thich: Because muons are much heavier than electrons, they orbit very close to protons, allowing for a clearer perception of the proton's size. The result of 0.84 femtometers instead of about 0.88 caused a stir, with some suggesting new physics. After nearly a decade, new measurements with regular hydrogen also yielded a small value, close to 0.84. Many scientists believe the puzzle has mostly been solved: the old measurements had errors that were not well understood.

cau_hoi: The Standard Model of particle physics consists of 17 fundamental particles. Which fundamental force is NOT described by this model?
giai_thich: The Standard Model includes 6 quarks, 6 leptons (such as electrons, muons, neutrinos), 4 force-carrying bosons (photon, gluon, W and Z), and the Higgs boson. It accurately predicts thousands of experimental results. However, it does not include gravitational force, does not explain dark matter, dark energy, why neutrinos have such small mass, or why the universe has more matter than antimatter. The hypothetical graviton that would carry gravitational force has never been detected.

cau_hoi: In 2022, the CDF group at Fermilab announced that the mass of the W boson is heavier than predicted. In 2024, which experiment at CERN will announce different measurement results that align with the Standard Model?
giai_thich: The CDF group analyzed data collected over about 10 years at the Tevatron accelerator with high precision, so the deviation in results attracted significant attention. However, measurements from ATLAS (2023) and CMS (2024) at the LHC both yielded values consistent with the Standard Model. This is an example showing that science requires multiple independent experiments before recognizing a "new discovery." The W boson mediates weak interactions, causing beta decay.

cau_hoi: In 2015, the LHCb experiment at CERN announced the discovery of which type of particle consisting of five quarks, predicted since the 1960s?
giai_thich: Protons and neutrons consist of three quarks, while mesons consist of one quark and one antiquark. Gell-Mann and Zweig suggested that combinations of four or five quarks are possible. Many previous claims of pentaquark discoveries in the early 2000s were not confirmed, leading to skepticism in the community. The 2015 result from LHCb has very high reliability. Since then, LHCb has discovered dozens of new particles, showing that the "particle zoo" is still very rich.

cau_hoi: In 2023, the ALPHA-g experiment at CERN answered what question about antimatter?
B: Antihydrogen falls down under the influence of gravity just like ordinary matter, not "falling up"
giai_thich: There is a hypothesis that antimatter could be repelled by gravity, explaining why the universe has little antimatter. To test this, scientists had to create antihydrogen atoms consisting of an antiproton and a positron, then hold them using a magnetic field in a vertical tube. As the magnetic field was gradually reduced, most of the antiatoms escaped downwards, just as general relativity predicted. Einstein's theory of relativity passed another test.

cau_hoi: In 1931, Paul Dirac pointed out that if "magnetic monopoles" (magnets with only one pole) exist, what must be true?
A: Electric charge in the universe must be a multiple of a smallest value, explaining why charge is quantized
C: All magnets will lose their magnetism
D: The Earth will lose its magnetic field
giai_thich: All magnets we know have two poles; cutting one in half still yields two poles. Dirac found that just one magnetic monopole somewhere in the universe would be enough to explain why all electric charges are multiples of the electron charge. On February 14, 1982, Blas Cabrera at Stanford University recorded a signal consistent with the expected magnetic monopole, jokingly called the "Valentine's Day monopole," but the signal never repeated. To date, no magnetic monopole has been confirmed.

cau_hoi: The brilliant Italian physicist Ettore Majorana predicted in 1937 which type of particle, before he mysteriously disappeared in 1938?
D: Majorana particle: a type of particle that is its own antiparticle
giai_thich: Fermi once ranked Majorana among geniuses like Galileo and Newton. In March 1938, he boarded a ship from Palermo to Naples and then disappeared, which remains a mystery to this day. Physicists are investigating whether neutrinos are Majorana particles. In superconducting materials, 'Majorana modes' are being sought to create stable qubits for quantum computers, but claims of discovery so far remain controversial.

cau_hoi: The hypothetical particle 'axion', proposed in the late 1970s and a candidate for dark matter, was named by Frank Wilczek after what?
A: The name of a Greek god
C: The name of a laundry detergent brand, because this particle 'cleans up' a problem in theory
giai_thich: The strong force theory allows for an asymmetry that experiments do not observe, called the 'strong CP problem'. In 1977, Roberto Peccei and Helen Quinn proposed a mechanism to resolve it, and Wilczek along with Steven Weinberg pointed out that it required a new particle. Wilczek remembered the detergent brand Axion. The ADMX experiment in the US is using a strong magnetic field to search for axions converting into microwave photons.

cau_hoi: In 1889, mathematician Henri Poincaré won the prize from King Oscar II of Sweden for his work on the 'three-body problem'. What was surprising?
A: He proved that three bodies can always remain stationary
C: He found an error in his own paper and from that discovered chaos: the orbits of three mutually attracting bodies are generally unpredictable by simple formulas
D: He proved that the Solar System would collapse tomorrow
giai_thich: Newton solved the two-body problem, like the Earth orbiting the Sun, but adding a third body complicates things significantly. After the paper was published, Poincaré discovered an important mistake. He personally funded the reprinting and recall of the old copies. The revised version contained the first ideas about chaos, nearly 70 years before Lorenz. The science fiction novel 'The Three-Body Problem' by Liu Cixin was inspired by this problem.

cau_hoi: In 1975, Mitchell Feigenbaum discovered the number approximately 4.669 appears in many different systems as they transition to chaos. What does this number describe?
A: The ratio at which 'period doubling' occurs closer together before the system becomes chaotic
B: The number of days in a lunar week
C: The distance from the Earth to the Sun
D: The number of atoms in a water molecule
giai_thich: Feigenbaum experimented with a HP-65 pocket calculator, patiently recalculating a simple formula. As he increased a parameter, the system transitioned from stable to oscillating between 2 values, then 4, 8, 16... with the distance between each doubling shrinking at a ratio of about 4.669. The remarkable thing is that this number is the same in dripping faucets, electrical circuits, and heated liquids. It is called the Feigenbaum constant, a 'universal constant' of chaos.

cau_hoi: The fine-structure constant, approximately equal to 1/137, describes what and why does it fascinate physicists?
A: The speed of light measured in km
B: The strength of the electromagnetic force, a dimensionless number that no one can explain why it has that value
C: The number of days in a year
D: The number of prime numbers in the periodic table
giai_thich: Because it is dimensionless, this constant has the same value whether we use meters or inches, seconds or hours. If it were slightly larger or smaller, stars and atoms might not form as they do now. Feynman called it 'one of the greatest mysteries of physics'. Wolfgang Pauli was obsessed with the number 137, and according to legend, he died in room number 137.

cau_hoi: In 1957, graduate student Hugh Everett III proposed which interpretation of quantum mechanics, later called 'many worlds'?
B: Only one possibility occurs as chosen by God
C: The universe is a video game
D: Every possibility of a quantum measurement occurs, each possibility in its own branch of the universe
giai_thich: According to Everett, the wave function never 'collapses' upon measurement; instead, the observer also superposes and the world splits into many non-communicating branches. The idea was ignored for many years, causing Everett to leave physics for military analysis. By the 1970s, Bryce DeWitt popularized it under the name 'many worlds'. Today, this is one of the popular interpretations, but it remains controversial because it cannot be directly tested.

cau_hoi: What does the 'no-cloning theorem' (1982) in quantum mechanics state?
A: It is impossible to create a perfect copy of an unknown quantum state
B: All particles are exactly the same
C: It is impossible to copy documents
D: It is impossible to clone animals
giai_thich: The theorem was proven by Wootters, Zurek, and Dieks in 1982. It has important implications: if an eavesdropper tries to read quantum information, they will inevitably change the state and be detected. This is the basis of quantum cryptography, such as the BB84 protocol proposed by Bennett and Brassard in 1984. The theorem also explains why 'quantum teleportation' always destroys the original state.

cau_hoi: What strange phenomenon does the 'quantum Zeno effect' describe?
A: An atom heats up when being observed
B: Continuously observing a quantum system can slow down or prevent its state change
giai_thich: The name comes from the Greek philosopher Zeno's paradox of the arrow, who argued that a flying arrow is actually stationary at each moment. In 1977, Misra and Sudarshan described the effect, and in 1990, David Wineland's group observed it with beryllium ions. The saying 'a watched pot never boils' has a real quantum version.

cau_hoi: What does the 'Unruh effect' (1976) predict about a person accelerating extremely in a vacuum?
C: That person will feel the vacuum as a warm thermal radiation bath, while a stationary person only feels the cold vacuum
giai_thich: Canadian physicist William Unruh pointed out that the concept of 'particles' depends on the observer. However, the effect is extremely small: to feel a temperature of just 1 K, one must accelerate at about 10²⁰ m/s², roughly 10 billion billion times Earth's gravity. The effect is closely related to Hawking radiation, as according to general relativity, being near a black hole is like accelerating. It has not been directly observed.

cau_hoi: The 'black hole information paradox', which has sparked debate since the 1970s, revolves around what question?
B: What color is a black hole
C: How heavy is a black hole
D: When a black hole evaporates via Hawking radiation, is the information about what fell into it lost forever, which quantum mechanics does not allow?
giai_thich: Hawking initially believed that information is lost, contradicting a fundamental principle of quantum mechanics. In 1997, Hawking and Kip Thorne bet John Preskill that information was lost; in 2004, Hawking conceded and gifted Preskill an encyclopedia of baseball, suggesting that information could be 'retrieved at will'. Today, many physicists believe information is preserved, but the exact mechanism is still under investigation.

cau_hoi: In 1997, Juan Maldacena proposed "AdS/CFT duality", the most cited paper in the history of high-energy physics. What is the main idea?
A: A theory with gravity in a higher-dimensional space is equivalent to a theory without gravity on the boundary of that space, similar to a three-dimensional image.
D: All objects have the same mass.
giai_thich: This is the most concrete example of the "holographic principle" proposed by Gerard 't Hooft and Leonard Susskind: information in a region of space can be encoded on the surface surrounding it, like a flat hologram containing a three-dimensional image. The duality allows physicists to solve very difficult problems about quark-gluon plasma and quantum materials by switching to easier black hole problems.

cau_hoi: String theory in physics assumes that fundamental particles are essentially what, and how many non-time dimensions are needed?
D: Tiny vibrating energy strings; need 10 dimensions (or 11 in M-theory).
giai_thich: Like vibrating strings at different notes, each mode of vibration of a string corresponds to a type of particle, including the graviton, allowing the theory to combine gravity with quantum mechanics. The additional dimensions are thought to be curled up so small that they are invisible. Strings are about the size of the Planck length, 10⁻³⁵ m. The biggest problem is that so far the theory has not made any experimentally verifiable predictions.

cau_hoi: Many physicists once hoped the LHC would find "supersymmetric" particles. What are the results so far?
B: Hundreds of supersymmetric particles have been found.
C: No supersymmetric particles have been found, forcing physicists to reconsider many models.
giai_thich: Supersymmetry posits that each known particle has a heavier "partner": the electron has a "selectron", the quark has a "squark". The theory is attractive because it could explain dark matter and why the Higgs particle is so light. However, after more than 10 years of collisions at the highest energies ever achieved, there are no signs. Some physicists who lost bets had to pay for bottles of wine. This does not completely rule out supersymmetry but pushes the hypothetical particles to higher masses.

cau_hoi: In 1925, student Ernst Ising solved the one-dimensional magnet model in his thesis. Why did the "Ising model" become very famous later?
B: The two-dimensional version, solved exactly by Lars Onsager in 1944, became a classic example of phase transition, widely applicable from magnets to neural networks.
C: Because the model explains the weather.
D: Because it is used to measure temperature.
giai_thich: The model consists of arrows pointing up or down on a grid, where each arrow wants to align with its neighbors. Ising could only solve the case of one row and found no phase transition, thinking the model was useless. But the two-dimensional case does have a real phase transition at a specific temperature. The model is used for alloys, liquids, and even crowd behavior, and is the basis for the Hopfield network that won the Nobel Prize in 2024.

cau_hoi: The 2016 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to David Thouless, Duncan Haldane, and Michael Kosterlitz for their use of topology. What does topology study?
B: Properties that do not change when continuously deformed, such as the number of holes in an object: a coffee cup with a handle and a donut both have one hole.
giai_thich: When presenting at the award announcement, the Nobel committee used a pretzel, a bagel, and a candy cane with two holes to explain. The number of holes only changes in whole steps, similar to how some properties of quantum materials change discretely. Scientists use this idea to explain phase transitions in thin films and quantum Hall effects. "Topological materials" promise less error-prone quantum computers.

cau_hoi: The 1972 article "More is Different" by physicist Philip Anderson presents what famous argument?
C: When many particles combine, new laws emerge that cannot be simply inferred from the laws of individual particles.
D: The more particles, the more similar they are.
giai_thich: Anderson opposed the view that knowing only the most fundamental laws is sufficient to understand everything. Knowing everything about a water molecule does not immediately tell us about ocean waves or snowflakes. Each complex layer, from chemistry to biology to psychology, requires its own concepts. Anderson won the Nobel Prize in 1977. He was also the first to describe the mechanism later called the Higgs mechanism when studying superconductors in 1962.

cau_hoi: "The butterfly effect", the idea that a butterfly flapping its wings in Brazil could cause a tornado in Texas, originates from the work of whom?
giai_thich: In 1961, Lorenz reran a weather model on a computer but entered the rounded number 0.506 instead of 0.506127. He was surprised to find that the results after a while were completely different. This is a characteristic of chaotic systems: extremely sensitive to initial conditions, making it impossible to predict the weather accurately beyond about two weeks. The term "butterfly effect" comes from his talk in 1972. The "Lorenz attractor" also looks like butterfly wings.

cau_hoi: In 1964, James Cronin and Val Fitch discovered that the neutral kaon violates which symmetry, a clue explaining why the universe has more matter than antimatter?
A: CP symmetry (combination of charge conjugation and mirror reflection).
giai_thich: After Wu showed that nature distinguishes left from right, physicists hoped that at least "switching particles with antiparticles and looking in a mirror" would keep everything the same. Cronin and Fitch found that kaons decay violating this, albeit only about 2 times in 1,000. The two received the Nobel Prize in 1980. However, the level of CP violation in the Standard Model is still too small to explain the excess matter in the universe.

cau_hoi: In 1967, Soviet physicist Andrei Sakharov proposed three conditions to explain what?
C: Why the Earth has a magnetic field.
D: Why the early universe produced more matter than antimatter, allowing galaxies and us to exist.
giai_thich: The three conditions are: there must be a process that changes the baryon number, violation of C and CP symmetry, and there must be a stage of thermal imbalance. If initially matter and antimatter were equal, they would annihilate each other, leaving only light. Just one extra matter particle over about a billion pairs is enough to create the universe we have today. Sakharov later became a human rights activist and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1975.

cau_hoi: "Planck length", about 1.6 × 10⁻³⁵ m, is considered by many physicists to be what?
B: The scale at which both quantum gravity becomes significant, and the concept of continuous space may no longer hold.
giai_thich: Planck calculated this length in 1899 by combining three natural constants: the gravitational constant, the speed of light, and Planck's constant. It is smaller than a proton by about 10²⁰ times. If you magnified an atom to the size of the entire observable universe, the Planck length would only be about the size of a tree. "Planck time", about 5.4 × 10⁻⁴⁴ seconds, is the time it takes light to travel that length, the earliest moment that current physics can discuss about the universe.

cau_hoi: In 1952, David Bohm proposed the 'pilot wave' interpretation of quantum mechanics with what idea?
A: Particles always have a definite position and are guided by a 'wave', predicting the same outcomes as conventional quantum mechanics
giai_thich: Louis de Broglie had a similar idea in 1927 but abandoned it due to criticism. Bohm's theory shows that 'hidden variables' are possible, as long as they are 'non-local', meaning the pilot wave connects everything instantaneously. This inspired John Bell to research and propose the famous inequality. In 2005, French scientists discovered bouncing oil droplets on a vibrating oil surface exhibited pilot wave-like behavior.

cau_hoi: Before 2019, an international team created the world's nearly perfect silicon-28 sphere for what purpose?
C: To count the number of atoms in the sphere to accurately determine Avogadro's constant, aiding the new definition of the kilogram
giai_thich: The sphere weighs about 1 kg and is so round that if enlarged to the size of Earth, the highest and lowest points would differ by only a few meters. Silicon was enriched to over 99.99% silicon-28 isotope so that all atoms are nearly identical. By measuring the diameter with lasers and the distance between atoms with X-rays, scientists counted about 2.15 × 10²⁵ atoms. This method and the Kibble balance yield consistent results.

cau_hoi: What is the famous title of Eugene Wigner's 1960 essay about the role of mathematics in physics?
B: "The unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences"
giai_thich: Wigner wondered why human-created mathematical structures, sometimes conceived purely for beauty, describe the world so accurately. For example, complex numbers were invented to solve equations, then became the core language of quantum mechanics. 19th-century non-Euclidean geometry became the foundation for general relativity. Wigner won the Nobel Prize in 1963 for applying symmetry theory to atomic nuclei.

cau_hoi: What strange phenomenon does John Wheeler's 1978 'delayed choice' experiment demonstrate?
A: The decision to measure wave or particle behavior can be made after the photon has passed through the slit, yet the result still matches that choice
B: Photons travel backward in time to change the past
D: Photons stop to wait for an observer
giai_thich: At first glance, it seems that the current choice 'changes' the past of the photon. However, according to quantum mechanics, no information is sent back in time: photons do not have a 'definite path' until measured. The experiment has been conducted with photons since 2007, and even with reflected light from satellites in 2017. Wheeler even imagined a universe version using light from a star being bent by a galaxy.

cau_hoi: In 1956, what did Robert Hanbury Brown and Richard Twiss discover when measuring light from Sirius?
D: Photons from a common light source tend to arrive at the detector in 'clusters' more than randomly
giai_thich: They used a mirror from an old military searchlight to measure the angular size of the star. The results sparked significant controversy as many physicists believed photons were independent of each other. Roy Glauber explained this using quantum theory of light, opening the field of quantum optics, and won the Nobel Prize in 2005. Today, particle physicists use the same idea to measure collision region sizes in accelerators.

cau_hoi: In 1987, the Hong – Ou – Mandel experiment sent two identical photons simultaneously into two sides of a beam splitter. What was the result?
B: Two photons always separate to two sides
C: Two photons always exit from one side, never each from a different side
giai_thich: According to classical probability, each photon has a 50% chance of passing through and a 50% chance of reflecting, so half the time they would exit in two different directions. However, those possibilities interfere and cancel each other out when the photons are identical. The coincidence rate at the two detectors drops nearly to zero, creating the famous 'Hong – Ou – Mandel dip'. This experiment is a fundamental tool for testing photon sources for optical quantum computers.

cau_hoi: "Kondo effect", explained by Jun Kondo in 1964, describes what strange phenomenon?
B: The resistance of certain metals with magnetic impurities increases as the temperature drops to very low levels
giai_thich: Normally, the colder a metal is, the lower its resistance due to less atomic vibration. However, since the 1930s, it has been observed that some metals like gold with iron impurities exhibit increased resistance at very low temperatures. Kondo, a Japanese physicist, pointed out that conducting electrons interact with the spins of impurity atoms. Solving the full problem required Kenneth Wilson's 'renormalization group' method, who won the Nobel Prize in 1982.

cau_hoi: According to simple band theory, some metal oxides should conduct electricity, but in reality, they are insulators. What is this phenomenon called?
D: Mott insulators: strong repulsion between electrons prevents them from moving
giai_thich: British physicist Nevill Mott explained in the 1930s – 1940s: each atom holds one electron, and for an electron to jump to an adjacent atom that already has an electron, it must 'pay' a very high energy cost. It's like a parking lot where each space already has a car, so no car can move. Interestingly, high-temperature superconductors made from copper oxide are created when 'doping' Mott insulators. Mott won the Nobel Prize in 1977.

cau_hoi: "Planck time", about 5.4 × 10⁻⁴⁴ seconds, has what significance for cosmologists?
A: It is the earliest time after the Big Bang that current physics can describe; before that, a quantum gravity theory is needed that does not yet exist
B: The time of one day on Mars
C: The time of a lightning strike
D: The time light takes to travel from the Sun to Earth
giai_thich: In the 'Planck era', the universe was hot and dense enough that all four fundamental forces may have unified into one. General relativity predicts a 'singularity' with infinite density, but most physicists believe this is a sign that the theory has broken down and does not describe reality. Candidates like string theory and loop quantum gravity are attempting to describe this phase. The number of Planck times in one second is vastly greater than the number of seconds since the Big Bang.

cau_hoi: Loop quantum gravity, another candidate besides string theory, suggests what about space?
C: Space is made up of tiny discrete 'space atoms' woven into a network, rather than being continuous
giai_thich: Physicists like Carlo Rovelli, Lee Smolin, and Abhay Ashtekar developed this theory since the late 1980s. Areas and volumes only take on discrete values, similar to the energy of electrons in atoms. Some models based on the theory predict the Big Bang could be a 'Big Bounce' from a previously contracting universe. Like string theory, this theory has yet to have direct experimental validation.

cau_hoi: In 1979, Sheldon Glashow, Abdus Salam, and Steven Weinberg received the Nobel Prize for unifying which two forces? Salam also became the first person from which group to win the Nobel Prize in Physics?
A: Gravitational and electromagnetic forces; the youngest person
B: Electromagnetic and weak interaction forces; the first Muslim to win a Nobel in science
C: Strong and weak forces; the first woman
D: Gravitational and strong forces; the first African
giai_thich: The weak force theory predicted the heavy W and Z bosons, discovered at CERN in 1983 by the team of Carlo Rubbia and Simon van der Meer, who received the Nobel Prize in 1984. Abdus Salam from Pakistan established the International Centre for Theoretical Physics (ICTP) in Trieste (Italy) in 1964 to assist scientists from developing countries. Many Vietnamese physicists have conducted research at ICTP.

cau_hoi: In 1971, graduate student Gerard 't Hooft and his advisor Martinus Veltman proved what, which helped them win the Nobel Prize in 1999?
C: The weak force theory can be 'renormalized', meaning it yields finite meaningful results instead of infinities
giai_thich: In quantum field theory, calculations often yield meaningless infinities. Renormalization is a technique that 'absorbs' infinities into a few measurable quantities like mass and charge. 't Hooft's proof made physicists truly believe in the theories of Glashow, Salam, and Weinberg. Veltman wrote the Schoonschip computer program to perform massive algebraic calculations, one of the first symbolic mathematics software.

cau_hoi: The 2004 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to David Gross, Frank Wilczek, and David Politzer for the discovery of 'asymptotic freedom' in 1973. What does this mean?
A: The strong force between quarks weakens when they are very close together and strengthens when pulled apart, like a rubber band
B: Quarks fly freely throughout the universe
C: Quarks have no force acting on them
D: The strong force is always constant
giai_thich: Unlike the electromagnetic force, which weakens with distance, the strong force increases when quarks are pulled apart. Thus, quarks are 'trapped' permanently in protons and neutrons: no matter how hard you pull, energy will create new quark-antiquark pairs instead of freeing a single quark. At high energies, quarks become almost free, explaining experiments of electron collisions with protons at Stanford. Wilczek was only 21 years old when he conducted this work.

cau_hoi: In 1973, Makoto Kobayashi and Toshihide Maskawa predicted what to explain CP violation, when only three types of quarks were known?
C: There are only two types of quarks
D: At least three generations of quarks must exist, meaning six types of quarks
giai_thich: At that time, physicists only knew about up, down, and strange quarks. Kobayashi and Maskawa pointed out that with two generations of quarks, CP violation could not occur, but with three generations, it could. The charm quark was discovered in 1974, the bottom quark in 1977, and the top quark in 1995, confirming the prediction. Experiments in Japan (Belle) and the USA (BaBar) in the early 2000s measured CP violation consistent with the theory. They received the Nobel Prize in 2008.

cau_hoi: Half of the 2008 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Yoichiro Nambu for discovering which mechanism related to how particles acquire mass?
giai_thich: Spontaneous symmetry breaking is like a pencil standing on its pointed end: all directions are equal (symmetric), but when it falls, it must choose a direction. The laws remain symmetric, but the actual state does not. Nambu was inspired by BCS theory of superconductivity to apply it to particle physics in 1960. This idea is foundational for the Higgs mechanism. Nambu is known for being ahead of his time by about 10 years.

cau_hoi: What happened to Peter Higgs' first paper in 1964 about the mass-generating mechanism?
